question: Explain and, if possible, demonstrate how to power the radio from an alternative battery or power source.
gold_answer: If the main service bank is depleted, the radio can normally be switched over to a separate emergency/domestic battery via the vessel's battery selector, or connected directly to a small dedicated emergency battery through a fused lead. Confirm 12 V nominal supply, check that the radio boots normally and that GPS is still available. On the training rig, disconnect the primary battery lead and connect the emergency lead in the same way, observing polarity and fuse rating.
expected_points: battery selector or dedicated emergency battery
radio boots and GPS still available
note any loss of GPS if it draws from another bus
answer: 1. power the radio from an alternative battery or power source. Outcome: the radio will operate effectively during emergencies. Warning: ensure the radio is powered before using it in an emergency situation.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Show how to verify that the correct channel list (for the operating region) is available on the set.
gold_answer: On the main display check the channel set indicator (INT, USA or CAN). Cycle through a few characteristic channels (e.g. Ch 22A, Ch 67, Ch 80) and confirm that they are present and correctly labelled for the region. If the set has a menu of channel groups (Atlantic, US, Canada) verify the correct one is selected. Cross-check against the almanac's channel list for the current operating area.
expected_points: check channel set indicator on the display
select correct channel group if applicable
answer: 1. verify channel list. Outcome: confirmation of the correct channel list being available. Warning: ensure the channel list matches the operating region.

section_title: Basics of Radio Installation and Use
question: Demonstrate shutting down the radio correctly while leaving it ready for the next operation.
gold_answer: Ensure Ch 16 (or the intended standby channel) is set, volume is at a normal level and squelch at threshold. Note the last known GPS position and UTC time in the log. Press and hold the power key until the display switches off. Verify no residual glow and that the DSC guard flap is closed. When the master switch is turned off, the settings will be preserved for the next start-up.
expected_points: set channel to Ch 16 before shutdown
normal volume and squelch at threshold
note position and UTC time in the log
press and hold power key to switch off
answer: 1. shut down the radio. Outcome: the radio is powered off and ready for the next operation. Warning: ensure the radio is powered off to avoid unnecessary battery drain.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Identify all components of the ship's radio installation: transceiver, antenna, power supply, GPS input, etc.
gold_answer: Point to and name each item: fixed VHF transceiver at the chart table; masthead VHF/DSC antenna; low-loss coaxial run and PL-259 connector; DC feed with fuse near the battery (typically 5–10 A) and battery isolator; GPS antenna or plotter feeding NMEA 0183/2000 to the radio; external cockpit speaker if fitted; DSC ground/RF earth. Confirm labels, cable runs and the ship station licence document held on board.
expected_points: fused DC feed and battery isolator
external cockpit speaker and ship station licence
answer: The excerpt covers the technical specifications and operational requirements for modern maritime communication systems. Outcome: effective communication with rescue services during emergencies. Warning: ensure all equipment is operational before departure.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to check the ship station's MMSI is correctly programmed into the DSC VHF.
gold_answer: On the DSC menu select 'MY MMSI' or 'STATION ID'. Confirm the nine-digit MMSI shown matches the ship station licence. Cross-check the first three digits (MID) against the flag state code — UK 232/233/234/235, Netherlands 244/245/246. If the MMSI is missing, showing 000000000 or the wrong number, do not send any DSC calls and note the issue; on most sets the MMSI can only be entered once and requires a manufacturer reset to change.
expected_points: MY MMSI or STATION ID menu entry
match to the ship station licence
note issue if missing or wrong
answer: 1. check the MMSI programming. Outcome: confirmation that the MMSI is correctly programmed. Warning: ensure the MMSI is correctly programmed to avoid communication issues.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to scroll through menu options to access DSC functions.
gold_answer: Press the MENU key or dedicated DSC key. Use the up/down channel keys or the rotary knob to scroll through the top-level entries — typically DISTRESS, INDIVIDUAL CALL, GROUP CALL, ALL SHIPS, MSI/POSITION REPORT, LOG. Press ENTER or the soft key labelled OK to open the selected item. ESC returns to the previous level. Practise navigating without transmitting until the layout is familiar.
expected_points: scroll with knob or up/down keys
top-level entries: DISTRESS, INDIVIDUAL, GROUP, ALL SHIPS, LOG
ENTER / soft key to open, ESC to go back
answer: 1. Scroll through the menu options. 2. Press the desired function key. Outcome: Accessing specific DSC functions. Warning: Ensure the MMSI number is correctly programmed for DSC functionality.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate setting up an individual DSC routine call to a specified MMSI.
gold_answer: Open DSC menu → INDIVIDUAL CALL → ROUTINE. Enter the target MMSI digit by digit (or select from the directory), then choose the proposed voice working channel (e.g. Ch 72). Press SEND / CALL. Wait for the receiving radio to acknowledge; both radios switch to the working channel. Then follow up by voice: "(other vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER."
expected_points: voice follow-up on the agreed channel
answer: 1. set up an individual DSC routine call. Outcome: successful communication with the called station. Warning: ensure the MMSI is correctly entered in the phone book.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to acknowledge a received routine DSC call and switch to the indicated working channel.
gold_answer: When a routine DSC call is received, the radio alarms, displays the caller's MMSI and the proposed channel. Press ACCEPT / ACK (or the soft key labelled ACK/ACCEPT). The radio automatically switches to the proposed channel; listen briefly, then reply by voice: "(caller), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL (…), OVER." If the channel is unsuitable, press REJECT and call the station manually on an alternative channel.
expected_points: radio alarms and displays MMSI and channel
voice reply on the working channel
answer: 1. switch to Channel 67. Outcome: successful communication with the called station. Warning: do not switch channels until instructed.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to set and confirm the vessel's position manually on the radio if GPS input fails.
gold_answer: On the DSC/position menu select MANUAL POSITION or POSITION ENTRY. Enter latitude (degrees, minutes and hemisphere N/S) and longitude (degrees, minutes and hemisphere E/W), plus the UTC time of the position, using the keypad. Save and confirm the entry — the radio now displays "MAN" or "USER" next to the position instead of "GPS". Update the manual position every few minutes while GPS is unavailable.
expected_points: enter UTC time of the position
display shows MAN or USER indicator
update every few minutes while GPS is unavailable
answer: 1. set the vessel's position manually. Outcome: accurate position is communicated effectively. Warning: ensure manual position entry is confirmed before transmission.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to view the DSC call log and identify the last received alert.
gold_answer: On the DSC menu open LOG or CALL LOG; select RECEIVED (or DISTRESS / URGENCY / SAFETY / ROUTINE as needed). Scroll to the most recent entry, press ENTER to view details: sender MMSI, category, time (UTC), position and follow-up channel. This lets the operator review missed alerts or reconstruct events after the fact. Some sets separate received and transmitted logs.
expected_points: most recent entry at the top
details: MMSI, category, time, position, channel
answer: 1. view the DSC call log. Outcome: identification of the last received DSC call. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is correctly programmed.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate switching between intership and port operation channels according to instructions.
gold_answer: Take the examiner's instruction ("switch to Ch 12 for port control") and select the channel using knob, up/down or keypad entry. Confirm the display shows the new number and that low power is selected if in a harbour. Announce the switch on the current channel first ("...GOING TO CHANNEL ONE TWO, OVER"), then on the new channel re-establish contact briefly.
expected_points: listen to the examiner's channel instruction
answer: 1. switch to the specified channel. Outcome: effective communication with the coast radio station or another ship. Warning: ensure the channel is clear before transmitting.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to adjust display brightness for day and night operations.
gold_answer: Use the BRIGHTNESS or DIM key (often a dedicated key or a short-press of the power button). Set full brightness in daylight so the display is readable under the spray hood; at night reduce brightness to preserve night vision but keep essential icons (channel number, DSC alarm) visible. Modern sets have a NIGHT MODE preset that also switches the backlight colour to red or amber.
expected_points: BRIGHTNESS / DIM key or short-press power
reduce at night for night vision
NIGHT MODE preset on modern sets
answer: 1. Adjust display brightness. Outcome: Improved visibility of the display in various lighting conditions. Warning: Ensure the display is adjusted for optimal visibility.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to test an internal speaker and any external loudspeaker if present.
gold_answer: Tune to a live channel with regular traffic (e.g. Ch 16 or a marina channel). Adjust internal volume and confirm audio is clear. Enable the external cockpit speaker (dedicated switch or menu) and adjust its volume, checking audibility at the helm and around the cockpit. Toggle between speakers to verify each works independently. If neither produces audio, check the AF/GAIN and check the speaker connector.
answer: 1. Test the internal speaker(s) and any external loudspeaker(s). Outcome: Confirmation of operational communication equipment. Warning: Do not operate the general emergency alarm until ordered by the officer of the watch.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to select and call a coast station using DSC from an onboard directory (if fitted).
gold_answer: Open DSC → DIRECTORY, select the coast station entry (e.g. HM COASTGUARD), which stores the coast station's MMSI. From there choose INDIVIDUAL CALL → ROUTINE, choose the voice working channel used by the coast station (e.g. Ch 67 for UK coastguard) and press SEND. When the coast station acknowledges, follow up by voice on the working channel.
expected_points: choose the coast station's voice working channel
answer: 1. select the MMSI number of the coast station. 2. press the Call key. Outcome: successful communication with the selected coast station. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is correctly selected before pressing Call.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to initiate a DSC test call where this is permitted (on simulator, not live).
gold_answer: On the training simulator open DSC → TEST CALL. Enter the target MMSI (typically a coast station MMSI that supports automatic DSC test replies) and press SEND. The simulator sends the test call and waits for the acknowledgement, which is displayed on the log. Live DSC test calls should only be made against stations that offer this service; misuse can cause SAR confusion.
expected_points: target MMSI (coast station that supports test)
live tests only against supporting stations
answer: 1. switch the transmitter to Channel 70. Outcome: successful initiation of a DSC test call. Warning: do not transmit distress or safety calls during testing.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to cancel an outgoing routine DSC call before it is sent.
gold_answer: During the composition step (after selecting the call type and before pressing SEND), press ESC / CANCEL to abort the call. If the SEND button has already been pressed but the radio is still in the pre-transmission countdown (some sets show a short delay), press CANCEL again — many DSC sets will still block the transmission. Once transmitted, the call cannot be recalled and, if incorrect, must be corrected by a follow-up call.
expected_points: also works during short pre-transmit countdown
correct by a follow-up call if needed
answer: 1. press the PTT button. 2. wait for a response. Outcome: the DSC call is successfully sent and acknowledged. Warning: ensure the DSC call is not sent if no response is received within a minute.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to configure a group call using a given group MMSI (if supported by equipment).
gold_answer: Open DSC → GROUP CALL → SETUP (or DIRECTORY entry for the group). Enter the nine-digit group MMSI (starting with a leading zero, e.g. 023201234) and store it under a memorable name (e.g. FLOTILLA-2026). To make the group call, select GROUP CALL → send, choose the working channel, and transmit. All correctly programmed radios alert and can switch to the working channel together.
expected_points: GROUP CALL SETUP or DIRECTORY entry
group MMSI starts with a leading zero
all group radios alert and can switch
answer: 1. select the appropriate MMSI number. Outcome: successful establishment of communication with the selected vessel. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is valid and accessible.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to access and interpret stored DSC distress alerts on the device.
gold_answer: Open DSC → LOG → RECEIVED DISTRESS. Scroll to select an entry and press ENTER to view: sender's MMSI (identifies the vessel), UTC time, nature of distress if selected, position, and follow-up channel. Cross-check MMSI against the vessel directory if available. Use the log to reconstruct incident history for the coastguard or an inquiry.
expected_points: details: MMSI, time, nature, position, channel
answer: 1. access the MMSI number. 2. review the list of recent calls. 3. check the logbook for previous communications. Outcome: successful communication with other vessels or shore stations. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is correctly set to avoid communication failures.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to temporarily disable DSC audible alarms and then re-enable them correctly.
gold_answer: When an alarm sounds, press the ALARM CANCEL / SILENCE key to mute the tone for the current alert while keeping the DSC watch active. To disable all alarms globally is generally not permitted on type-approved sets — but volume can be reduced via the DSC audio volume setting. Always re-check that the alarm is re-enabled at full volume immediately after the temporary silencing, so the next alert is heard.
expected_points: ALARM CANCEL / SILENCE for current alert only
cannot globally disable on type-approved sets
reduce alarm volume via DSC audio setting
answer: 1. temporarily disable DSC audible alarms. 2. re-enable DSC audible alarms. Outcome: improved clarity in communication during distress situations. Warning: failure to re-enable DSC alarms may result in missed distress calls.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to confirm the ship station is configured for Sea Area A1 operation.
gold_answer: Confirm the VHF/DSC set is powered, has GPS input, is on Ch 70 DSC watch and Ch 16 voice watch, and that the MMSI matches the ship station licence. For Sea Area A1 the DSC-VHF combination plus (recommended) an EPIRB is sufficient — no MF/HF or Inmarsat is required. Cross-check the ship station licence entry showing 'A1' or equivalent.
expected_points: DSC watch on Ch 70 and voice watch on Ch 16
no MF/HF or Inmarsat required for A1
answer: 1. confirm ship station configuration. Outcome: clarity on the operational status of the ship station. Warning: ensure the ship station is configured correctly before departure.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to access context-sensitive help or quick menus if available on the radio.
gold_answer: Many modern sets have a HELP or ? soft key that shows a short description of the currently selected menu entry. Others provide quick menus via a long-press on a specific key. Demonstrate opening one such menu on the training rig, review the visible options, and explain how to use the built-in help to remind the operator of DSC steps without needing the paper manual.
expected_points: HELP or ? soft key on many sets
long-press for quick menu on others
supports DSC step reminders under stress
answer: 1. press the key(s) in sequence. Outcome: access to context-sensitive help or quick menus. Warning: ensure keys are pressed correctly.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Show how to check the supply voltage as displayed by the radio (if such a feature exists).
gold_answer: On the STATUS or DIAGNOSTIC menu of many modern radios the current supply voltage is displayed. Note the value — a nominal reading is 12.6–13.8 V under charge, and below 11 V the radio may reset during a distress transmission. If the voltage is low, investigate the battery bank, fuses and cabling before departure. If the feature does not exist, use the vessel's battery monitor as a proxy.
expected_points: STATUS / DIAGNOSTIC menu shows supply voltage
investigate battery, fuses, cabling if low
use vessel battery monitor if no on-radio feature
answer: 1. check the supply voltage. Outcome: confirmation of adequate power supply for the radio. Warning: ensure the supply voltage is within the specified range to avoid damage to the equipment.

section_title: Functionality of the Ship Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate and explain the correct use of any integrated AIS display functionality related to communications, if present.
gold_answer: On radios with integrated AIS the operator can view a list of nearby AIS targets by MMSI, name, CPA and TCPA. Selecting a target lets the operator send a DSC individual call directly to that vessel's MMSI (useful for coordinating a passing manoeuvre with a large ship). Demonstrate opening the AIS list, selecting one target, and initiating an INDIVIDUAL CALL from it. Confirm the correct MMSI is loaded into the DSC call.
expected_points: AIS target list with MMSI and name
select target to send DSC individual call
confirms MMSI in the call setup
useful for passing arrangements with commercial traffic
answer: 1. select the appropriate channel. Outcome: successful communication with the designated station. Warning: ensure the channel is clear before transmitting.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to switch the handheld VHF on and off.
gold_answer: To switch on, press and hold the power button (usually combined with the volume knob) for 1–2 seconds until the display lights up and the boot self-test completes. To switch off, press and hold the same button for 2–3 seconds until the display fades. Confirm any battery-low warning at start-up. Do not simply pull the battery — the settings need a clean shutdown to be preserved.
expected_points: power button (often combined with volume knob)
press and hold to switch on
press and hold longer to switch off
answer: 1. Switch the handheld VHF on and off. Outcome: The VHF radio is operational for communication. Warning: Ensure the VHF radio is switched on before use.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to check the battery charge level on a handheld unit.
gold_answer: The display normally shows a small battery icon divided into segments. Full segments indicate full charge; one or two segments indicate imminent low-battery. Some handhelds also show voltage in the STATUS menu. A separate BATTERY TEST option, where fitted, briefly loads the battery and reports capacity. If low, replace the battery pack or place the unit on the charger and use the other handheld for the current watch.
expected_points: battery icon with segments on display
one or two segments = low battery
voltage in STATUS menu on some sets
replace or charge if low, use backup for watch
answer: 1. check the battery charge level. Outcome: confirmation of battery status and readiness for communication. Warning: ensure batteries are charged before use.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to change channels on the handheld.
gold_answer: Use the up/down channel keys, the rotary knob or the direct keypad entry (where fitted). Confirm the new channel number on the display. On many handhelds a dedicated Ch 16 (or Ch 16/9) key returns instantly to the calling channel. Confirm the correct channel set (INT/USA/CAN) matches the region of operation.
answer: 1. press the channel button. Outcome: the display shows the selected channel. Warning: do not hold the channel button for more than 3 seconds.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to set the handheld to high or low power and explain when each should be used.
gold_answer: Press the H/L key (or its soft-menu equivalent) to toggle between high (typically 5–6 W) and low (typically 1 W) power. Use high power for offshore calls, coast station contact and any distress or urgency traffic; use low power inside a marina, alongside another vessel or when talking to nearby crew ashore. Low power both saves battery and reduces interference on shared channels.
expected_points: high ~5–6 W for offshore and distress
low ~1 W in marina, short range
answer: 1. Set the handheld to high power for long-range communication. 2. Set the handheld to low power for close-range communication. Outcome: Effective communication over appropriate ranges. Warning: High power is not necessary for close-range communication.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate adjusting volume and squelch on the handheld radio.
gold_answer: Rotate the volume knob (often combined with the power button) or use the volume up/down keys until traffic is audible over background noise. Rotate the squelch knob (or menu entry) fully open, then gradually close until the background noise just disappears ("squelch threshold"). If reception of a distant station is expected, back off the squelch slightly. Re-check with a real transmission where possible.
expected_points: open squelch fully then close to threshold
answer: 1. Adjust the volume control knob. 2. Turn the squelch knob until static noise disappears. Outcome: Clear communication is established. Warning: Overheating may occur if the radio is held too close to the speaker.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to attach and secure the handheld's antenna.
gold_answer: Align the antenna's BNC or SMA thread with the handheld's connector, screw or push-lock it fully home, and confirm no play or wobble. Never transmit without the antenna attached — this can damage the transmitter output stage. Inspect the antenna for cracks, corrosion or a bent base and replace if damaged. For range use the supplied full-length antenna rather than a short 'stubby' where possible.
expected_points: BNC or SMA connector, fully home
inspect for cracks, corrosion, bent base
answer: 1. attach the handheld antenna. Outcome: improved communication range. Warning: ensure the antenna is properly attached to avoid signal loss.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate correct microphone and speaker positioning on the handheld while speaking.
gold_answer: Hold the handheld vertically or at a slight angle away from the body, with the microphone (usually behind the front-panel grille) about 5 cm from the mouth and slightly off-axis. Speak at a normal conversational volume. During reception, hold the speaker close to the ear or angled towards the operator to hear over ambient noise. Do not cover the antenna with your hand — it detunes the signal.
expected_points: hold vertically or slight angle away from body
mic ~5 cm from mouth, slightly off-axis
answer: 1. hold the microphone about 2 inches from your mouth. Outcome: clear communication with the station. Warning: do not touch the red button while holding the microphone.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to select channel 16 and then return to a previously used working channel.
gold_answer: Press the dedicated Ch 16 (or 16/9) key to jump directly to Channel 16 — this works from any other channel. To return to the previously used channel, press the same key again (many handhelds toggle back to the last channel used), or use LAST CHANNEL / RECALL if provided, or manually re-select the channel. Confirm the new channel number on the display each time.
expected_points: dedicated Ch 16 key for instant access
press again or use LAST CHANNEL to toggle back
answer: 1. select Channel 16. 2. press the PTT button. 3. say 'co-ordination call on Channel'. 4. wait for a response. Outcome: successful communication with the coast station. Warning: do not forget to return to Channel 16 after the call.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to operate any waterproofing seals or covers (e.g., for charging ports).
gold_answer: Locate the rubber flap covering the charging or accessory port. Open by lifting the flap gently at the tab (not the connector itself); after use, press the flap firmly into its seat until it clicks / seats flush. Inspect the seal for dirt, sand or damage before closing — a compromised seal is a common cause of water ingress. After sea use rinse the handheld with fresh water with the flap closed.
expected_points: open by lifting tab, not connector
press firmly back into seat until flush
inspect seal for dirt and damage
rinse in fresh water with flap closed after sea use
answer: 1. operate the power switch. 2. press the transmit button. Outcome: successful communication over the radio. Warning: do not touch the antenna while transmitting.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to secure the handheld to prevent loss overboard (lanyard, clip, etc.).
gold_answer: Attach the supplied wrist lanyard to the eyelet on the handheld and loop it around the wrist during use. When stowed, use the belt clip and clip to the harness or a lifejacket lanyard point. Consider a floating case for extra buoyancy. Do not carry a handheld loose in a pocket without a secondary tether. Regularly check the eyelet and lanyard for wear.
expected_points: belt clip to harness or lifejacket
never loose in pocket without tether
check eyelet and lanyard for wear
answer: 1. secure the handheld. Outcome: the handheld is safely secured and ready for use. Warning: ensure the handheld is properly secured to avoid loss.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate the charging procedure for the handheld battery.
gold_answer: Insert the battery pack into the correct orientation on the charging cradle (or plug the charging cable into the handheld's charging port) and connect the charger to the 12 V or mains supply. Verify the charging indicator LED (usually red = charging, green = full). Do not charge in extreme temperatures. Once fully charged, disconnect and store the handheld ready for the next watch — some Li-ion chemistries prefer partial rather than 100% charge for storage.
expected_points: connect charger to 12 V or mains
LED indicators for charging and full
disconnect and store ready for next watch
answer: 1. charge the handheld battery. Outcome: the battery is fully charged and ready for use. Warning: do not touch the contacts of the battery.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to change a battery pack safely on the handheld unit.
gold_answer: Switch the handheld off. Release the battery-pack latch (a lever, screw or slide depending on the model) and pull the pack straight off the back. Check the contacts on both battery and handheld for cleanliness and no corrosion. Fit the new pack in the correct orientation, confirming the latch clicks home. Power on and confirm normal operation, then log the swap.
expected_points: fit new pack in correct orientation
power on and confirm normal operation
answer: 1. remove the battery pack. 2. disconnect the antenna cable. Outcome: the battery pack is successfully changed and the antenna cable is disconnected. Warning: ensure the battery pack is disconnected before changing it.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to perform a radio check using the handheld from deck.
gold_answer: On deck, extend the antenna vertically, select an appropriate working channel (e.g. Ch 9 or a marina channel), and call a known station: "(station), THIS IS (own vessel handheld), RADIO CHECK, OVER." Wait for the signal report. Repeat with the fixed radio for comparison. Do not use Ch 16. Note that handheld range is much lower than the masthead antenna's — do not expect the same report.
expected_points: compare with fixed radio; range naturally lower
answer: 1. perform a radio check. Outcome: confirmation of effective communication capability. Warning: ensure all equipment is operational before departure.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to use any available scan or dual-watch function on the handheld.
gold_answer: Access SCAN or DW/TRI-WATCH via a dedicated key or menu. Scan cycles through all channels stored in the scan list, pausing on any active channel. Dual-watch monitors Ch 16 (or the priority channel) plus one selected working channel simultaneously — useful when waiting for a marina call while at anchor. Turn scan off before transmitting, since scan is paused during PTT.
expected_points: SCAN cycles through all stored channels
DW / TRI-WATCH monitors Ch 16 plus working channel
use DW at anchor waiting for a marina
answer: 1. use any available scan or dual-watch function. Outcome: effective monitoring of multiple channels simultaneously. Warning: do not exceed the number of channels specified by Ofcom.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to reduce squelch temporarily to check for weak signals.
gold_answer: Rotate the squelch knob anti-clockwise (or press the monitor button, where fitted) so the squelch fully opens — background noise (hiss) is heard. Listen for a few seconds; any faint voice traffic will now be audible. Once satisfied, return the squelch to threshold. Do not leave the squelch open — continuous noise fatigues the operator and drains the battery on receive.
expected_points: rotate squelch anti-clockwise or press MONITOR
do not leave squelch open (fatigue, battery drain)
answer: 1. adjust squelch knob. 2. reduce squelch setting. Outcome: improved ability to detect weak signals. Warning: reducing squelch may increase static interference.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to stow the handheld correctly when not in use to protect it from damage.
gold_answer: Switch off, close any port flaps and secure the antenna. Stow in a dedicated wall-mount holder or a padded soft case in a dry, ventilated locker near the companionway — accessible in an emergency but protected from spray, sun and impact. Do not stow in a pocket with loose keys, or near strong magnets. Charge fully before stowing for long periods.
expected_points: switch off and close port flaps
answer: 1. stow the handheld safely. Outcome: the handheld is protected from damage and remains accessible for emergencies. Warning: do not stow the handheld in a lifejacket pocket.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate using the handheld for intership communication between two training vessels.
gold_answer: On the calling channel (Ch 16 or agreed Ch 9), call the other vessel three times, THIS IS your vessel three times, OVER. Agree an intership working channel (e.g. Ch 72), both switch and re-establish contact. Use low power for close range, keep the message brief, and close with OUT once done. Return listening watch to Ch 16 on both handhelds.
expected_points: use low power for close range
answer: 1. switch to working channels. Outcome: effective communication between vessels regarding navigation and safety. Warning: do not exceed the allowed number of working channels.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Show how to clean contacts and seals on the handheld unit if needed.
gold_answer: Remove the battery. Wipe the metal battery-pack and handheld contacts with a soft dry cloth or a cotton bud very lightly moistened with isopropyl alcohol — never abrasive material. Inspect and gently clean the rubber flap seals with fresh water and a soft cloth; check for cracks or missing rubber. Re-fit the battery only when everything is dry, and confirm normal power-on.
expected_points: soft dry cloth or isopropyl on cotton bud
clean rubber seals with fresh water
answer: 1. Clean contacts and seals on the handheld unit if needed. Outcome: Improved communication quality. Warning: Do not touch the contacts of the handheld unit.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Demonstrate how to check that the handheld is set to the correct channel set (INT/USA/CAN, if present).
gold_answer: Open the SETUP or CHANNEL SET menu, note the currently selected channel set (INT, USA, CAN) on the main display, and change if required. Verify by scrolling to a characteristic channel — e.g. Ch 22A should exist only in USA, Ch 88 in INT. Confirm the change persists after power-cycle. Choosing the wrong channel set is one of the most common cross-border errors.
expected_points: current set shown on main display
answer: 1. Check that the handheld is set to the correct channel set (INT/USA/CAN, if present). Outcome: The handheld is ready for immediate communication. Warning: Ensure the handheld is set correctly to avoid confusion.

section_title: Functionality of the Handheld Station Equipment
question: Explain and demonstrate the limitations of range when using the handheld from different points on the vessel.
gold_answer: Handheld range is limited by antenna height and body absorption. From the cockpit at deck level (~1 m) expect 3–5 nm to another handheld; from the mast steps (~5 m) up to 8–10 nm; below decks the range drops sharply. Position the operator with a clear view towards the intended recipient, keep the antenna vertical, and hold the handheld away from body and metal structures. Do not rely on a handheld for offshore distress alerting.
expected_points: range limited by antenna height and body absorption
not a substitute for fixed VHF offshore
answer: The range of communication is affected by the height of the antenna. The range of communication increases with the height of the antenna. Outcome: effective communication between vessels. Warning: the range of communication is limited by the height of the antenna.

question: On a simulator, demonstrate sending a DSC distress alert with correct category and position.
gold_answer: On the simulator open DSC → DISTRESS. Select the nature of distress (e.g. SINKING, FIRE, COLLISION) if time allows; otherwise leave as UNDESIGNATED. Confirm GPS position is present. Lift the guard flap and press and hold the red distress button until the confirmation tone (typically 3–5 seconds). The simulator sends the alert on Ch 70 with MMSI, position, time and category, then automatically switches to Ch 16 for the voice follow-up.
expected_points: select nature of distress if time
press and hold the red button 3–5 s
auto-switch to Ch 16 for voice follow-up
answer: DSC distress alerts can be sent using MMSI numbers or voice procedures. Outcome: effective communication of distress situations. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is correctly programmed for DSC functionality.

question: Immediately after, perform the associated MAYDAY voice call on the designated voice channel.
gold_answer: On Ch 16 transmit: "MAYDAY, MAYDAY, MAYDAY, THIS IS (vessel name x3), MMSI (…), CALLSIGN (…), MAYDAY (vessel name), POSITION (lat/long or bearing/distance from a fixed point), NATURE OF DISTRESS (e.g. sinking after collision), ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, (…) POB, ADDITIONAL INFORMATION (safety equipment on board), OVER." Speak slowly and clearly.
expected_points: THIS IS + vessel name x3, MMSI/callsign
answer: MAYDAY is used for distress situations only. Outcome: effective communication of distress information to rescue services. Warning: MAYDAY must be used only in life-threatening situations.

question: Demonstrate repeating the MAYDAY call after no response is heard for a specified period.
gold_answer: If no acknowledgement is heard within about 15 seconds, repeat the full MAYDAY call unchanged. If still no answer after several attempts, repeat again from the DSC — some sets automatically retransmit the DSC distress alert every few minutes until acknowledged. Continue monitoring Ch 16 and Ch 70 between calls. If a coast station is unreachable, transmit MAYDAY RELAY on behalf of yourself as if you were a third party (some SRC procedures teach a modified relay).
expected_points: monitor Ch 16 and Ch 70 between calls
MAYDAY RELAY if coast station out of range
answer: 1. repeat MAYDAY every 4 minutes. Outcome: increased visibility of distress signals to rescue services. Warning: failure to repeat MAYDAY may result in delayed assistance.

question: Show how to respond by voice to a MAYDAY call from another vessel as a nearby ship offering assistance.
gold_answer: Wait to let the coast station or MRCC acknowledge first. If no acknowledgement is heard after a reasonable interval (~5 minutes in Sea Area A1) and you can help, transmit on Ch 16: "(distress vessel name), THIS IS (own vessel), RECEIVED MAYDAY, MY POSITION (…), ETA TO YOUR POSITION (…), STATE OF READINESS (…), OVER." Continue to keep the MRCC informed once they take control.
expected_points: offer assistance if no ACK after ~5 minutes
cooperate with MRCC once they take control
answer: 1. respond to the MAYDAY call. Outcome: effective communication with the vessel in distress. Warning: do not divert attention away from the distress call.

question: Demonstrate how to acknowledge a distress relay from a coast station without interfering with control of traffic.
gold_answer: When a coast station issues MAYDAY RELAY, remain silent unless specifically called. If you can assist and the coast station invites acknowledgement, transmit: "(coast station), THIS IS (own vessel), RECEIVED MAYDAY RELAY OF (time UTC), MY POSITION (…), READY TO ASSIST, OVER." Do not attempt to acknowledge to the distress vessel directly — the coast station is in control.
expected_points: acknowledge only to the controlling coast station
state received MAYDAY RELAY and time
do not talk directly to the distress vessel
answer: 1. acknowledge the distress relay. Outcome: effective communication of distress information. Warning: do not interfere with traffic control during distress communications.

question: Show the correct use of the phrase SEELONCE MAYDAY under examiner guidance.
gold_answer: The distress vessel or the controlling coast station may impose silence on the channel: "SEELONCE MAYDAY, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS (vessel), SEELONCE MAYDAY, OUT." Then only the distress vessel, the controlling station and specifically requested assisting stations may transmit. Silence is lifted with SEELONCE FEENEE (silence lifted) or partially relaxed with PRUDONCE (limited resumption). Note pronunciation: SAY-LONSS MAY-DEE.
expected_points: imposed by distress vessel or controlling coast station
SEELONCE MAYDAY, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS ..., SEELONCE MAYDAY, OUT
only distress and controlling stations may transmit
answer: 1. show the phrase 'SEELONCE MAYDAY'. Outcome: the examinee demonstrates proficiency in using the phrase 'SEELONCE MAYDAY' correctly. Warning: incorrect use of phrases may lead to penalties during examinations.

question: Demonstrate cancelling a false DSC distress alert on the simulator and then issuing a MAYDAY CANCELLED voice message.
gold_answer: On the simulator use DSC → DISTRESS CANCEL if available. Then on Ch 16 transmit: "ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel name x3, MMSI), POSITION (…), CANCEL MY DISTRESS ALERT OF (UTC time), REASON (e.g. inadvertent activation), NO ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, THIS IS (vessel), OUT." Confirm the cancellation with the coast station and log the event with time, reason and coast station response.
expected_points: ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS + vessel + MMSI
CANCEL MY DISTRESS ALERT OF (UTC time) with reason
confirm with coast station and log
answer: 1. cancel the distress alert using DSC. 2. confirm cancellation by voice. Outcome: the distress alert is successfully cancelled. Warning: ensure all crew members are aware of the distress situation before cancelling the alert.

question: Show how to log the key details of a distress communication (time, position, vessel name, nature of distress).
gold_answer: In the radio or deck log record: UTC time of the initial alert, channel used (Ch 70 DSC + Ch 16 voice), sender's MMSI/callsign and name, position (lat/long), nature of distress, POB, coast station involved, key MRCC instructions, and time of cancellation or termination. Keep entries factual and chronological. The log may later be reviewed by the coastguard or an inquiry.
expected_points: MRCC instructions and time of termination
answer: 1. log the key details of the distress communication. Outcome: effective communication of distress information. Warning: ensure all details are logged accurately.

question: Demonstrate maintaining a listening watch on the distress channel during an ongoing SAR scenario.
gold_answer: Keep the radio on Ch 16 at all times during the SAR operation, with volume set well above ambient noise and squelch at threshold. Keep DSC watch active on Ch 70. Do not transmit unless invited or providing a scheduled update. Note any instructions to shift to a working channel and comply. If required to leave the helm, hand over the watch to another SRC-qualified crew member.
expected_points: hand over watch if leaving the helm
answer: 1. maintain a listening watch on Channel 16. Outcome: effective communication with rescue services during a distress situation. Warning: failure to maintain a listening watch may delay rescue operations.

question: Practice transferring control of distress communication from ship to coast station once instructed.
gold_answer: On the coast station's instruction ("(vessel), THIS IS (COASTGUARD), I TAKE CONTROL, OVER") acknowledge with "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), CONTROL TRANSFERRED, OVER" and then continue to answer their questions and follow their directions. Do not initiate new priority messages unless the situation changes materially. Log the time of transfer. This releases the operator from having to lead the traffic while remaining actively involved.
expected_points: coast station announces I TAKE CONTROL
do not initiate new priority messages unless the situation changes
answer: 1. transfer control of distress traffic. Outcome: effective coordination of distress communication between ship and coast stations. Warning: ensure all communications are acknowledged before transferring control.

question: Demonstrate repeating essential information (position, persons on board) clearly when requested by MRCC.
gold_answer: On MRCC's request, respond promptly and slowly: "THIS IS (vessel), MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO DEGREES ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE MINUTES NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE DEGREES FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE MINUTES WEST, POB FIVE, INCLUDING ONE INJURED, I SAY AGAIN, POSITION FIVE ZERO ... , POB FIVE, OVER." Use digit-by-digit pronunciation, decimal instead of point, and I SAY AGAIN to guarantee the copy.
expected_points: voluntary I SAY AGAIN for critical facts
answer: 1. repeat essential information. Outcome: improved clarity in communication regarding position and crew status. Warning: ensure all relevant information is communicated clearly to avoid misunderstandings.

question: Show how to brief crew on their roles during simulated distress communication.
gold_answer: Assign roles clearly before the simulation: one person on the radio (MAYDAY delivery, MRCC dialogue), one on the DSC/GPS confirming position, one on lookout and preparing safety equipment (liferaft, EPIRB, grab bag), one in charge of casualty if any. Rehearse the sequence with the MAYDAY card and confirm each role knows their trigger. Debrief after the drill to identify improvements.
expected_points: assign radio, DSC/GPS, lookout, casualty roles
rehearse the sequence with a MAYDAY card
answer: 1. Brief crew on their roles in distress communication. Outcome: Crew is aware of their responsibilities during distress situations. Warning: Failure to brief crew may result in confusion during actual distress situations.

question: Demonstrate switching from the initial distress channel to a working channel when directed by MRCC.
gold_answer: On MRCC's instruction ("(vessel), THIS IS (COASTGUARD), CHANGE TO CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER"), acknowledge ("(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), GOING TO CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER") and switch. On the new channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER." MRCC then continues coordination there, freeing Ch 16 for further distress traffic if needed.
expected_points: frees Ch 16 for other distress traffic
answer: 1. switch to Channel 69. Outcome: effective communication with the MRCC regarding distress situations. Warning: do not switch channels unless directed by the MRCC.

question: Show how to relay a distress call from another vessel that you hear weakly, according to proper format.
gold_answer: On Ch 16 transmit: "MAYDAY RELAY, MAYDAY RELAY, MAYDAY RELAY, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (own vessel x3), MMSI (…), FOLLOWING RECEIVED FROM (distress vessel name), POSITION (as heard), NATURE OF DISTRESS (as heard), TIME OF ORIGINAL CALL (UTC), OVER." Follow up any coast station acknowledgement with additional detail as it becomes available.
expected_points: MAYDAY RELAY x3, ALL STATIONS x3
THIS IS + own vessel and MMSI
state what was received from the distress vessel
cooperate with coast station on further detail
answer: 1. repeat the distress call. Outcome: the distress call is effectively communicated to rescue services. Warning: ensure the distress call is repeated clearly and accurately.

question: Demonstrate giving periodic updates on the vessel's situation during an ongoing distress.
gold_answer: Every 5–10 minutes (or when the situation changes materially), transmit an update: "MAYDAY, THIS IS (vessel), UPDATE — (vessel is now taking water in the forecabin), (crew members are wearing life jackets), (life raft ready to launch), (POB still five), OVER." Keep updates factual and short so MRCC can maintain accurate situational awareness.
expected_points: update every 5–10 minutes or on material change
answer: 1. report your position. 2. report your present course and speed. 3. report your present engine status. 4. report your present steering gear status. Outcome: improved situational awareness among crew members regarding the vessel's condition. Warning: failure to report may lead to confusion during emergencies.

question: Show how to terminate distress communications when instructed by MRCC and return to routine watch.
gold_answer: MRCC will announce: "ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (COASTGUARD), SEELONCE FEENEE, TIME (UTC), OUT." Acknowledge on request, then resume routine listening watch on Ch 16 and DSC on Ch 70. Log the time and reason for termination, the assisting units involved, and any lessons learned. Consider a short crew debrief once the situation is safe.
answer: 1. terminate distress communications. Outcome: the vessel is relieved of distress status. Warning: ensure all distress communications are terminated before returning to routine watch.

question: Demonstrate the correct use of the radio in a simulated abandon-ship scenario.
gold_answer: Before abandoning, send a DSC distress alert with nature ABANDONING SHIP and a full voice MAYDAY on Ch 16 stating the intention and time to abandon. Take a handheld VHF (and EPIRB, PLB, SART if available) into the liferaft. Once in the raft, keep the handheld VHF dry and switched off until you have reason to transmit — battery life is precious. Use the handheld to talk to SAR units on Ch 16 during approach.
expected_points: voice MAYDAY stating intention and time
take handheld VHF, EPIRB, PLB, SART
keep handheld off in liferaft to save battery
use handheld to talk to SAR on Ch 16 during approach
answer: 1. switch on the general emergency alarm. Outcome: all crew members are alerted to the emergency situation. Warning: failure to respond may result in immediate evacuation.

question: Show how to coordinate with another assisting vessel via VHF during the SAR exercise.
gold_answer: On Ch 16 (or the working channel assigned by MRCC), exchange positions, courses, speeds and intended actions with the other assisting vessel using SMCP structure. Agree on the search pattern (parallel, expanding square) and the reporting interval. Keep messages brief and coordinated with MRCC's overall picture — often one of the vessels is designated as On-Scene Coordinator (OSC).
expected_points: agree search pattern and reporting interval
answer: 1. confirm readiness for transfer. Outcome: successful transfer of personnel between vessels. Warning: ensure safety equipment is available before transfer.

question: Demonstrate handling of simultaneous incoming DSC distress alerts and selecting the one to respond to under guidance.
gold_answer: If two DSC distress alerts arrive at once (simulator scenario), silence both alarms, list them by MMSI and position, and consult the coast station on Ch 16 for direction. MRCC will typically instruct which vessel to prioritise based on immediacy of danger, proximity of your vessel and available SAR units. Do not attempt to respond to both simultaneously.
expected_points: silence alarms and list both by MMSI/position
typically based on danger and proximity
do not respond to both at once
answer: 1. handle simultaneous incoming DSC distress alerts. Outcome: successful response to the distress alert. Warning: do not interrupt the distress traffic on Channel 16.

question: Show how to conduct a short debrief explaining what went well and what could be improved in the distress exercise.
gold_answer: After the exercise gather the crew, review the sequence of events on the log, and structure the debrief around three questions: what worked (correct pro-words, quick DSC action, clear MRCC contact); what did not (slow position readouts, missed I SAY AGAIN, forgotten POB); what to change next time (rehearse MAYDAY card, pre-programme MRCC MMSI, improve GPS accuracy). Record the actions and revisit at the next drill.
expected_points: review log and sequence of events
three questions: what worked, what did not, what to change
answer: 1. conduct a short debrief. Outcome: participants understand the effectiveness of their communication during the distress exercise. Warning: ensure all safety equipment is operational before departure.

question: On a simulator, perform a PAN PAN voice call for loss of engine power in a busy fairway.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (lat/long), URGENCY: TOTAL LOSS OF ENGINE POWER IN CENTRAL FAIRWAY, DRIFTING WITH TIDAL SET TO NORTH-EAST AT 2 KNOTS, POB FOUR, VESSEL SAILING VESSEL 12 METRES, REQUEST TUG ASSISTANCE, OVER." Await MRCC response and follow their instructions.
expected_points: PAN PAN x3 and ALL STATIONS x3
answer: 1. switch to Channel 16. Outcome: successful communication with the coast radio station regarding engine problems. Warning: do not exceed the speed limit in the fairway.

question: Demonstrate how to update the coastguard when a tug has arrived to assist after a PAN PAN call.
gold_answer: On the assigned working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), UPDATE — TUG (name) IS ALONGSIDE AT POSITION (…), TOW COMMENCING TO (destination), URGENCY TRAFFIC ENDS AT MY NEXT TRANSMISSION, THIS IS (vessel), OVER." MRCC will normally clear the urgency traffic once the tow is under way and the risk is no longer immediate.
expected_points: update on the assigned working channel
answer: 1. make a MAYDAY call. 2. make a MAYDAY relay call. 3. make a MAYDAY acknowledgement. Outcome: effective communication of distress situations. Warning: do not make a MAYDAY call unless in grave and imminent danger.

question: Show how to send a DSC urgency alert (if available on training equipment) and then follow up with voice.
gold_answer: On the DSC menu select URGENCY → ALL SHIPS (or a specific coast station MMSI). Confirm GPS position, select follow-up channel Ch 16, and send. On Ch 16 immediately transmit the PAN PAN voice message with all standard elements: identification, position, nature, assistance, POB, OVER. The DSC alert primes the receiving stations for the voice PAN PAN.
expected_points: DSC URGENCY → ALL SHIPS or specific MMSI
confirm GPS position and follow-up channel
immediately follow up with voice PAN PAN on Ch 16
DSC primes receivers for the voice message
answer: 1. send a DSC urgency alert. 2. switch to Channel 16 or an appropriate working channel. 3. make a voice urgency call. Outcome: the Coastguard is alerted to the emergency situation. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is correctly programmed in the DSC.

question: Demonstrate issuing PAN PAN MEDICO for an injured crew member, including all relevant medical details.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "PAN PAN MEDICO x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), MEDICAL SITUATION — MALE CREW MEMBER AGED FORTY FIVE, SUSPECTED HEART ATTACK, CONSCIOUS BUT WEAK, PULSE ONE HUNDRED, BREATHING DIFFICULT, PATIENT IS COMFORTABLE AND WEARING LIFE JACKET, REQUEST MEDICAL ADVICE AND POSSIBLE EVACUATION, POB FIVE, OVER." Speak clearly, then follow MRCC instructions.
expected_points: PAN PAN MEDICO x3 and ALL STATIONS x3
answer: 1. issue PAN PAN MEDICO. Outcome: immediate attention from the coast radio station and medical advice. Warning: failure to provide essential information may delay assistance.

question: Show how to downgrade a situation from PAN PAN to routine once the immediate danger has passed.
gold_answer: On the working channel used with MRCC: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), SITUATION UNDER CONTROL, URGENCY TRAFFIC ENDS, PATIENT RECOVERED, NO ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, THANK YOU, OUT." MRCC will formally clear the urgency traffic and, if appropriate, close the case. Log the time and outcome. Any further follow-up (medical debrief, coastguard incident report) is handled routinely.
expected_points: update on the working channel with MRCC
state urgency traffic ends and reason
answer: 1. request medical assistance. Outcome: medical assistance is provided promptly. Warning: ensure safety before transferring patients.

question: Demonstrate how to call a coast station to ask whether an urgency message is appropriate before transmitting.
gold_answer: If unsure whether the situation warrants PAN PAN, call the coastguard first on their working channel (e.g. Ch 67 in the UK): "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), ROUTINE, REQUEST ADVICE, OVER." Describe the situation factually. The coastguard will advise whether to escalate to a formal PAN PAN, remain routine or take other action. This avoids over- or under-reaction.
expected_points: call coastguard on their working channel
answer: 1. call the coast station. 2. ask if an urgency message should be sent. Outcome: confirmation of whether an urgency message needs to be sent. Warning: do not send an urgency message unless requested by the coast station.

question: Perform a simulated urgency call for loss of steering gear in open water.
gold_answer: "PAN PAN, PAN PAN, PAN PAN, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), URGENCY: TOTAL LOSS OF STEERING GEAR, DRIFTING WITH WIND AT 15 KNOTS TOWARDS COAST, AMPLE SEA ROOM AT PRESENT, POB FOUR, MOTOR CRUISER 10 METRES, REQUESTING ASSISTANCE OR TOW, OVER." Follow the MRCC's directions.
expected_points: PAN PAN x3 and ALL STATIONS x3
nature of urgency: loss of steering
answer: 1. perform a simulated urgency call. Outcome: effective communication of distress situations. Warning: ensure all safety equipment is operational before departure.

question: Demonstrate providing clear and calm updates about the vessel's drift and conditions during the urgency scenario.
gold_answer: Every few minutes on the assigned channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), UPDATE — POSITION (…), DRIFT NOW EAST-NORTH-EAST AT 1.5 KNOTS, WIND 15 KNOTS, DISTANCE TO COAST FIVE MILES AND CLOSING, OVER." Keep the tone calm and factual. If a change requires escalation to MAYDAY (e.g. imminent grounding), announce it clearly.
expected_points: announce escalation to MAYDAY if needed
answer: 1. report your position. 2. report your present course and speed. 3. report your present drift. 4. report wind force and direction. Outcome: improved situational awareness among crew regarding the vessel's status and environmental conditions. Warning: ensure all crew members are aware of the current situation to prevent accidents.

question: Show how to respond as a nearby vessel when hearing a PAN PAN call that you are well-placed to assist.
gold_answer: After the coast station has responded (or if there is no response after a reasonable interval), transmit: "(distress vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), RECEIVED PAN PAN, MY POSITION (…), ETA TO YOUR POSITION (…), READY TO ASSIST, OVER." Then keep the coast station informed. Do not attempt to take over MRCC's role — offer help and follow their coordination.
expected_points: wait for coast station response if practical
answer: 1. acknowledge the distress call. Outcome: the vessel in distress receives confirmation of assistance from nearby vessels. Warning: ensure all communications are clear and understood by the vessel in distress.

question: Demonstrate how to request towing assistance via a PAN PAN call without overstating the danger.
gold_answer: Deliver the PAN PAN using factual language: state the failure (engine, steering, etc.), the current drift and sea room, and clearly state "REQUEST TOW" as the assistance needed. Do not use words like "sinking" or "in distress" unless they are literally true. This gives MRCC an accurate picture and avoids unnecessary escalation of SAR assets.
answer: 1. make a PAN PAN call. Outcome: effective communication of distress situations. Warning: do not overstate the danger when requesting towing assistance.

question: Show how to log details of an urgency communication and subsequent developments.
gold_answer: Record in the log: UTC time of PAN PAN, channel used, coast station MMSI/name, position, nature of urgency, POB, assistance requested, MRCC instructions received, any assisting vessels or tugs (names / MMSIs), time when situation was downgraded and reason. Keep entries factual and chronological. This log will be needed for any coastguard incident report or insurance claim.
expected_points: UTC time of PAN PAN and channel
answer: 1. log details in the ship's log. Outcome: all relevant information is recorded for future reference. Warning: ensure all communications are logged to avoid loss of information.

question: Perform a scenario where a minor medical issue slowly escalates and you decide when to issue PAN PAN.
gold_answer: Track vital signs and behaviour; if the crew member's condition deteriorates (loss of consciousness, chest pain, severe bleeding), that is the moment to escalate. Announce PAN PAN MEDICO as described, giving updated symptoms and clearly stating what has changed since the last observation. If deterioration continues towards a life-threatening state, further escalate to MAYDAY.
expected_points: trigger PAN PAN MEDICO on clear deterioration
answer: 1. assess the situation. Outcome: appropriate response is taken based on the assessment. Warning: do not jump overboard if the lifeboat/liferaft is not immediately alongside.

question: Demonstrate use of clear position reporting (GPS and visual references) during the urgency call.
gold_answer: Give position in two forms: GPS latitude/longitude digit by digit with hemisphere, and a visual reference (bearing and distance from a known headland, buoy or lighthouse). Example: "POSITION FIVE ZERO DEGREES ONE TWO DECIMAL FOUR MINUTES NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE DEGREES FOUR SIX DECIMAL ONE MINUTES WEST, TWO POINT FIVE MILES SOUTH OF ANVIL POINT LIGHT." Two forms guard against a single-source error.
expected_points: visual bearing and distance from a fixed reference
answer: 1. report your position using GPS and visual references. Outcome: effective communication of your location to rescue services. Warning: ensure accurate position reporting to avoid confusion.

question: Show how to coordinate with harbour control regarding an urgency situation inside a port area.
gold_answer: On the port control channel (e.g. Ch 12): "(PORT NAME) PORT CONTROL, THIS IS (vessel), URGENCY: LOSS OF ENGINE INSIDE HARBOUR ENTRANCE, POSITION (…), DRIFTING, POB (…), REQUEST TUG OR ASSISTANCE, OVER." Port control will typically coordinate a workboat, warn incoming and outgoing traffic, and issue holding instructions. Keep the port control channel priority, comply with instructions and log all exchanges.
expected_points: port control coordinates workboat and warns other traffic
answer: 1. request harbour control. Outcome: successful coordination of operations and safety measures. Warning: ensure all safety equipment is operational before departure.

question: Demonstrate switching between distress and urgency channels if directed by MRCC.
gold_answer: MRCC may instruct: "(vessel), THIS IS (COASTGUARD), CHANGE TO CHANNEL SIX SEVEN FOR CONTINUED URGENCY TRAFFIC, OVER." Acknowledge with "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), GOING TO CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER", then switch and re-establish contact on the new channel. This frees Ch 16 for other priority traffic while urgency coordination continues quietly on the working channel.
expected_points: re-establish contact on the new channel
frees Ch 16 for other priority traffic
answer: 1. switch to Channel 69. Outcome: effective communication with MRCC regarding distress situations. Warning: do not switch channels unless directed by MRCC.

question: Perform a role-play where you must explain to crew why PAN PAN, not MAYDAY, is being used.
gold_answer: Briefly explain to the crew: "We have engine failure but we have sea room and no immediate life threat, so this is an urgency situation. I am sending PAN PAN, which asks for help but does not trigger the full SAR muster of a MAYDAY. If the situation gets worse — if we start drifting onto a lee shore or begin taking water — we escalate to MAYDAY." This clarifies priorities and defines the escalation trigger.
expected_points: PAN PAN asks for help without full SAR muster
MAYDAY is reserved for grave and imminent danger
answer: PAN PAN indicates an urgent situation that is not life-threatening. MAYDAY is reserved exclusively for grave and imminent danger. Outcome: the coastguard responds promptly to the distress call. Warning: MAYDAY should only be used in life-threatening situations.

question: Show how to request an updated weather forecast from a coast station during an urgency scenario.
gold_answer: On the coastguard working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), REQUEST LATEST WEATHER FORECAST FOR (sea area / region), OVER." The coastguard may either quote the current forecast or direct you to a scheduled MSI broadcast channel and time. Log the received forecast and integrate it into the ongoing decision-making (drift, tug arrival ETA, escalation threshold).
expected_points: call coastguard on their working channel
coastguard quotes forecast or directs to MSI channel
answer: 1. request an updated weather forecast. Outcome: improved situational awareness regarding weather conditions. Warning: ensure the weather forecast is requested at least twice if not received initially.

question: Demonstrate how to cancel an urgency condition once a tow or rescue vessel has taken control.
gold_answer: On the assigned working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), URGENCY TRAFFIC ENDS, TUG (name) IN CONTROL, TOW TO (destination) UNDER WAY, POB (…), NO FURTHER ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, THANK YOU, OUT." MRCC will formally close the urgency and stand down other units. Log the closure time, tug details and destination.
expected_points: update on the assigned working channel
answer: 1. confirm if the vessel is in distress. Outcome: clarification of the vessel's status and immediate assistance. Warning: ensure the vessel is not in distress before confirming.

question: Show how to repeat key information slowly and clearly on request from the coast station.
gold_answer: On any request "SAY AGAIN YOUR POSITION" or "SAY AGAIN POB", respond promptly and slowly, digit by digit where numerical: "THIS IS (vessel), MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO DEGREES ONE TWO DECIMAL SIX MINUTES NORTH, POB IS FIVE, I SAY AGAIN, POB FIVE, OVER." Do not rush and do not paraphrase. Repetition confirmed by the coastguard means the correct information has been captured.
expected_points: digit by digit for numerical data
voluntary I SAY AGAIN for critical facts
answer: 1. repeat key information slowly and clearly. Outcome: effective communication of essential details. Warning: ensure clarity in communication to avoid misunderstandings.

question: Perform a debrief explaining the reasoning behind choosing PAN PAN for the scenario.
gold_answer: Debrief with the crew: "The scenario had a serious mechanical failure but no immediate risk to life, so PAN PAN was the correct call. If we had been drifting onto rocks with only minutes of sea room, or had a life-threatening medical, we would have gone straight to MAYDAY. The choice reflected the ITU classification of grave and imminent danger (MAYDAY) versus urgency (PAN PAN)." Record the reasoning in the log for future reference.
expected_points: scenario had no immediate life threat
PAN PAN was the correct call
MAYDAY reserved for grave and imminent danger
answer: PAN PAN indicates an urgent situation that is not life-threatening. OVER indicates the end of a transmission and invites a response. Outcome: effective communication of urgency regarding the disabled vessel. Warning: do not use MAYDAY when there is no immediate danger to life.

question: Perform a SECURITÉ call to warn of unlit fishing nets in an area you are leaving.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: UNLIT FISHING NETS OBSERVED IN POSITION (lat/long), APPROXIMATELY FIVE HUNDRED METRES OF NET, MARKED ONLY BY SMALL FLOATS, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, OUT." Then contact the coastguard on a working channel to relay the position for rebroadcast.
expected_points: SÉCURITÉ x3 and ALL STATIONS x3
state NAVIGATIONAL WARNING and net position
follow up with coastguard for rebroadcast
answer: 1. perform a SECURITÉ call. Outcome: increased awareness among nearby vessels about the presence of unlit fishing nets. Warning: unlit fishing nets pose a danger to navigation.

question: Demonstrate relaying a significant navigational hazard report to coastguard using SECURITÉ.
gold_answer: After the SÉCURITÉ broadcast on Ch 16, call the coastguard on their working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), REPORTING NAVIGATIONAL HAZARD, POSITION (…), DESCRIPTION (…), TIME OBSERVED (…), REQUEST YOU REBROADCAST, OVER." The coastguard will normally include the report in the next scheduled MSI or NAVTEX transmission and log the hazard in the local warning database.
expected_points: call coastguard on their working channel
included in next MSI or NAVTEX
answer: 1. report the position of the wreck. Outcome: improved situational awareness among nearby vessels. Warning: the wreck is in a dangerous position.

question: Show how to request repetition of a SECURITÉ weather forecast from a coast station.
gold_answer: On the coastguard working channel used for the broadcast: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), REQUEST YOU REPEAT SAFETY BROADCAST OF (time), SEA AREA (…), OVER." The coast station will re-transmit the missed portion. Do not request repetition on Ch 16 itself. Log the received forecast and integrate it into planning.
expected_points: request on the coast station's working channel
answer: 1. request repetition of the SECURITÉ weather forecast. Outcome: improved clarity in weather information communication. Warning: ensure all weather warnings are noted and acted upon immediately.

question: Demonstrate how to log a received safety broadcast that affects your planned route.
gold_answer: In the log record: UTC time received, channel, coast station identity, brief summary of the hazard or warning (type, position, effect on navigation), and the action taken (course change, extra watch, reduction in sail). Plot the hazard on the chart if practical. Note any subsequent updates or cancellations. This gives an evidential trail if the hazard later becomes an incident.
expected_points: plot on chart and note updates
answer: 1. log the safety message in the ship’s log. Outcome: all crew members are informed of the safety warning. Warning: safety broadcasts may require immediate action or avoidance of certain areas.

question: Perform a safety call to inform nearby traffic about your restricted manoeuvrability during towing operations.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), COURSE ZERO NINE ZERO, SPEED THREE KNOTS, VESSEL RESTRICTED IN ABILITY TO MANOEUVRE DUE TO TOWING OPERATIONS, TOWING (name of towed vessel) ASTERN, LENGTH OF TOW (…) METRES, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, OUT." Repeat every 30 minutes while the operation continues.
expected_points: state RESTRICTED IN ABILITY TO MANOEUVRE
identify towed vessel and tow length
advise vessels to keep clear; repeat every 30 min
answer: 1. perform a safety call. Outcome: nearby vessels are informed of the vessel's restricted manoeuvrability and potential danger. Warning: do not overtake when manoeuvring is restricted.

question: Show how to respond to a SECURITÉ message requesting vessels to keep clear of a SAR area.
gold_answer: Note the position and extent of the SAR area, plot it on the chart, and adjust the passage plan to keep well clear (typically at least 2 nm unless the message states otherwise). Reduce speed and post an extra lookout. If your route inevitably passes near the area, call the coastguard on their working channel to confirm safe transit or an alternative route. Log the message and the action taken.
expected_points: note position and extent of SAR area
plot on chart, adjust passage plan
reduce speed and post extra lookout
call coastguard if route passes near
answer: 1. respond to the SECURITÉ message. Outcome: increased safety for vessels in the vicinity of the accident. Warning: keep clear of the position marked by rockets / smoke buoys.

question: Demonstrate how to broadcast a safety message about a drifting object dangerous to navigation.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: LARGE DRIFTING TIMBER OBSERVED IN POSITION (lat/long) AT (time UTC), APPROXIMATELY FIFTEEN METRES LONG, HALF-SUBMERGED, DRIFTING NORTH-EAST, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, OUT." Follow up with coastguard on a working channel for rebroadcast and logging.
expected_points: advise keep clear; follow up with coastguard
answer: 1. broadcast a safety message. Outcome: increased awareness of the danger among nearby vessels. Warning: the area is dangerous due to a drifting object.

question: Perform a scenario where you transmit a safety message advising of reduced visibility in a narrow channel.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: FOG IN (channel name), VISIBILITY LESS THAN TWO HUNDRED METRES, WIND CALM, VESSELS ADVISED PROCEED WITH CAUTION AND MAINTAIN LISTENING WATCH ON CHANNEL ONE SIX, OUT." Update every 30 minutes or when conditions change materially.
expected_points: update every 30 min or on change
answer: 1. transmit a safety message. Outcome: all vessels in the area are informed about the safety situation. Warning: reduced visibility may affect navigation safety.

question: Show how to receive and acknowledge MSI (Maritime Safety Information) relevant to your voyage.
gold_answer: Once the coastguard's SÉCURITÉ announcement on Ch 16 directs listeners to the MSI working channel, switch to that channel and listen to the full text — no acknowledgement is expected during the broadcast. Log the relevant portions (gale warning, hazard position, NAVTEX message ID) and cross-check on the chart. If a specific portion was missed, request repetition on the working channel afterwards.
expected_points: listen to SÉCURITÉ announcement on Ch 16
log relevant portions and cross-check on chart
answer: 1. receive MSI on DSC. Outcome: timely receipt of important navigational warnings and meteorological information. Warning: ensure you have a DSC-equipped radio for receiving MSI.

question: Demonstrate how to switch channels when instructed to listen to a scheduled safety broadcast.
gold_answer: When the coastguard announces on Ch 16: "...ALL STATIONS SHIFT TO CHANNEL SIX TWO, SIX THREE OR SIX FOUR, OVER.", switch to the announced channel using knob, up/down or keypad entry. Confirm the display shows the new number. Listen to the broadcast, log key content and return to Ch 16 watch afterwards. Some sets do this automatically via NAVTEX-style scheduling.
answer: 1. switch to Channel 16. Outcome: successful communication with the Coastguard regarding safety broadcasts. Warning: do not interrupt safety broadcasts.

question: Perform a SECURITÉ message regarding a malfunctioning navigation light on your own vessel that may confuse others.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), COURSE (…), SPEED (…), SAFETY INFORMATION: MY STARBOARD NAVIGATION LIGHT NOT WORKING, TEMPORARY REPLACEMENT (torch/emergency light) IN USE, REQUEST VESSELS APPROACHING FROM MY STARBOARD SIDE MAINTAIN EXTRA CAUTION, VESSEL WILL PROCEED TO NEAREST HARBOUR, OUT." Repeat if the situation persists.
expected_points: request extra caution from other vessels
answer: 1. broadcast a SECURITÉ message. Outcome: increased awareness among other vessels and authorities about the navigation hazard. Warning: the navigation light is malfunctioning and may confuse other vessels.

question: Show how to coordinate with harbour control when reporting a small oil spill seen near the entrance.
gold_answer: On port control channel (e.g. Ch 12): "(PORT) HARBOUR CONTROL, THIS IS (vessel), REPORTING AN OIL SLICK NEAR THE HARBOUR ENTRANCE, POSITION (…), APPROXIMATELY (size) SQUARE METRES, DRIFTING (direction), NO SOURCE VESSEL IN SIGHT, OVER." Provide any additional info (colour, sheen, smell). Harbour control will task pollution response and may broadcast a warning to other vessels.
expected_points: call port control on its channel
report position and size of slick
follow up as tasked by harbour control
answer: 1. report the position of the oil spill. Outcome: effective communication regarding the oil spill and its location. Warning: ensure the oil spill is reported accurately to avoid navigational hazards.

question: Demonstrate how to phrase a safety message without causing undue alarm.
gold_answer: Use factual language and standard SMCP structure. State the hazard, position, effect on navigation and advised action. Avoid words like "emergency", "disaster" or subjective phrases such as "very dangerous" — the SÉCURITÉ prefix already signals priority. Example: "...NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: DRIFTING CONTAINER IN POSITION (…), APPROXIMATELY 6 METRES LONG, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR..." is calm and specific.
answer: 1. phrase the safety message clearly. Outcome: effective communication of safety information. Warning: do not cause undue alarm or unnecessary traffic.

question: Perform role-play where you repeat a safety message to another vessel that missed it.
gold_answer: On the vessel's working channel (or if urgent, on Ch 16): "(vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), RELAY OF SAFETY MESSAGE — NAVIGATIONAL WARNING RECEIVED FROM COASTGUARD AT (time UTC): DRIFTING CONTAINER IN POSITION (…), VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, OVER." Give the other vessel time to acknowledge and offer to repeat if needed. Log the relay.
expected_points: include time and content of the original
answer: 1. repeat the safety message. Outcome: all vessels receive the safety information. Warning: ensure all safety messages are acknowledged.

question: Show how to adjust radio procedures depending on whether you are originating or merely relaying safety information.
gold_answer: When originating, use the SÉCURITÉ prefix on Ch 16 and provide direct observation data (what you saw, when, where). When relaying an existing safety message from another station, identify the original source (e.g. "RECEIVED FROM COASTGUARD AT (time)"), so the recipient knows the information is second-hand. The distinction affects accountability and the recipient's assessment of currency.
expected_points: originating: SÉCURITÉ prefix with direct observation
relaying: identify original source and time
state the message content verbatim if possible
answer: 1. adjust radio procedures for safety information. Outcome: effective communication of safety messages. Warning: ensure safety information is communicated clearly and effectively.

question: Demonstrate good logging practices for safety messages, including source, time, and content summary.
gold_answer: Log entries should include: UTC time received or transmitted, channel, source (coastguard, other vessel or own observation), message category (navigational warning, weather warning, SAR area, MSI), content summary (position, hazard type, effect), and action taken by the vessel (course change, extra watch, relay). Keep entries factual and chronological to support subsequent audits or coastguard follow-up.
