answer: 1. log all safety messages. Outcome: improved safety awareness among crew regarding navigational hazards. Warning: ensure all safety messages are logged to avoid oversight.

question: Perform a simulated response where you divert the vessel's route based on a received safety broadcast.
gold_answer: After receiving the SÉCURITÉ (e.g. drifting container in your planned route), plot the hazard on the chart, calculate a safe passing distance (typically ≥ 2 nm), plan the new course and communicate the plan to the crew. If required, notify VTS or harbour control of the diversion: "(VTS), THIS IS (vessel), IN VIEW OF HAZARD REPORTED AT (time), DIVERTING NORTHWARD TO PASS AT LATITUDE (…), OVER." Log the change.
expected_points: plot hazard and plan safe passing distance (≥ 2 nm)
brief the crew on the new plan
answer: 1. divert course. Outcome: improved safety for vessels in the area. Warning: strong winds and heavy seas in area.

question: Show how to query a coast station for clarification about a hazard mentioned in a previous safety broadcast.
gold_answer: On the coast station's working channel: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), REGARDING NAVIGATIONAL WARNING BROADCAST AT (time UTC), REQUEST CLARIFICATION OF (specific element, e.g. exact position, duration of warning), OVER." The coast station will provide the requested detail. Log the response and update the passage plan accordingly.
expected_points: call on coast station's working channel
reference the original broadcast by time
answer: 1. listen to the safety broadcast. 2. make a safety call on Channel 16. 3. switch to a working channel after hailing. Outcome: successful communication with a coast radio station regarding navigation hazards. Warning: do not forget to switch channels after hailing.

question: Demonstrate how to advise nearby vessels of your participation in clearance work (e.g., debris removal) via SECURITÉ.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "SÉCURITÉ x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), SAFETY INFORMATION: CONDUCTING DEBRIS REMOVAL OPERATION IN AREA (…), ESTIMATED DURATION (…), VESSEL RESTRICTED IN ABILITY TO MANOEUVRE, VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR OF THE AREA, OUT." Repeat every 30 minutes or when conditions change. Coordinate with harbour control if inside a port area.
expected_points: state RESTRICTED IN ABILITY TO MANOEUVRE
coordinate with harbour control if in port
answer: 1. Advise nearby vessels of your participation in clearance work. Outcome: Nearby vessels are informed and can adjust their operations accordingly. Warning: Ensure safety during clearance work.

question: Perform a brief verbal debrief on how safety communications reduce environmental and collision risks.
gold_answer: Debrief: "SÉCURITÉ broadcasts alert every vessel in range to hazards — drifting containers, oil slicks, narrow-channel obstructions, weather deterioration — giving them time to alter course, reduce speed or reroute before an incident occurs. Over time this proactive dissemination measurably reduces collisions, groundings and pollution incidents, and supports pollution response by triggering shore action quickly."
expected_points: time to alter course or reduce speed
answer: Safety communications can reduce environmental pollution and collision risks. Effective communication requires clear language and understanding of roles. Outcome: improved safety during navigation. Warning: failure to communicate effectively may lead to environmental pollution and collisions.

question: Make a routine call to a marina to request a berth, providing all relevant vessel details.
gold_answer: On the marina's published channel (e.g. Ch 80 in the UK): "(Marina), (Marina), (Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), OVER." On reply: "(Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), TWELVE METRES LOA, TWO METRES DRAUGHT, MONOHULL SAILING YACHT, ETA ONE SIX ZERO ZERO UTC, REQUEST OVERNIGHT BERTH, POB THREE, OVER." Confirm assigned berth: "ROGER, BERTH C SEVEN, ARRIVING AT ONE SIX ZERO ZERO UTC, THANK YOU, OUT."
expected_points: call marina on published channel (e.g. Ch 80)
answer: 1. make a routine call on Channel 9. Outcome: successful communication with the marina regarding berth requests and weather warnings. Warning: do not exceed the speed limit in specified areas.

question: Demonstrate a routine call to a fuel dock to arrange refuelling on arrival.
gold_answer: "(Fuel dock), THIS IS (Vessel), ETA ONE FIVE MINUTES, REQUEST ONE FIVE ZERO LITRES DIESEL, WATER TOP-UP, STARBOARD SIDE ALONGSIDE, OVER." On confirmation: "THIS IS (Vessel), ROGER, WILL CALL TWO MINUTES OUT, OUT." Two minutes before arrival: "(Fuel dock), THIS IS (Vessel), TWO MINUTES OUT, OVER." Keep messages short and structured.
answer: 1. make a routine call to the fuel dock. Outcome: successful arrangement of refuelling and cargo operations. Warning: ensure all safety equipment is available before loading.

question: Perform a ship-to-ship routine call to coordinate a passing arrangement in a narrow channel.
gold_answer: On Ch 13 (bridge-to-bridge) or Ch 16 if 13 unavailable: "(target vessel), (target vessel), (target vessel), THIS IS (own vessel) x3, OVER." On reply propose channel: "REQUEST SWITCH TO CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." On the working channel, use SMCP: "(target), THIS IS (own vessel), INTENTION: I INTEND TO OVERTAKE YOU ON YOUR STARBOARD SIDE, SPEED (…) KNOTS, OVER." Await confirmation and log the exchange.
expected_points: initial contact on Ch 13 (bridge-to-bridge) or Ch 16
answer: 1. perform a ship-to-ship routine call. Outcome: successful coordination of passing arrangements between vessels. Warning: ensure all safety equipment is operational before departure.

question: Show how to move from channel 16 to a working channel when instructed during a routine call.
gold_answer: On Ch 16 the other station may say: "...REQUEST SWITCH TO CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." Reply: "(other station), THIS IS (own vessel), GOING TO CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." Switch, then re-establish contact: "(other station), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." Conduct the conversation and close with OUT, returning both stations to Ch 16 watch.
expected_points: close with OUT and return to Ch 16 watch
answer: 1. call the coast radio station on channel 16. Outcome: successful communication with the coast radio station. Warning: do not forget to change channels after the call.

question: Demonstrate a call to harbour control requesting permission to enter and berth.
gold_answer: On port control channel (e.g. Ch 12): "(PORT NAME) HARBOUR, THIS IS (vessel) x3, OVER." On reply: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (vessel), SAILING YACHT, TWELVE METRES LOA, TWO METRES DRAUGHT, POSITION TWO MILES SOUTH OF ENTRANCE, ETA ONE TWO ZERO ZERO UTC, REQUEST PERMISSION TO ENTER AND BERTH IN VISITOR AREA, OVER." Wait for the entry instruction and readback the assigned berth or holding position.
expected_points: call harbour control on its channel
answer: 1. request permission to enter. Outcome: permission is granted for entering the fairway. Warning: do not enter without permission.

question: Perform a routine call to a yacht club to confirm race start times and instructions.
gold_answer: On the club's working channel (per Sailing Instructions, e.g. Ch 72): "(Club), THIS IS (Vessel), CONFIRMING START TIME FOR (class), OVER." On reply: "(Club), THIS IS (Vessel), UNDERSTOOD START TIME ONE THREE ZERO ZERO UTC, CLASS FLAG (colour/description), THANK YOU, OUT." Log the start time and class flag for the crew brief.
expected_points: use club's working channel per SI
readback start time and class flag
answer: 1. perform a routine call. Outcome: confirmation of race details and safety information. Warning: ensure all safety equipment is operational before departure.

question: Show how to conduct a brief radio check with a known station without misusing distress channels.
gold_answer: On a working channel (e.g. Ch 9 or the marina's working channel): "(Station), THIS IS (Vessel), RADIO CHECK, OVER." On reply: "(Vessel), THIS IS (Station), READ YOU LOUD AND CLEAR, OVER." Reply: "THIS IS (Vessel), THANK YOU, OUT." Do not test on Ch 16. If a formal signal report is provided, note it in the log.
answer: 1. make a radio check on Channel 9. Outcome: confirmation of communication capability. Warning: do not misuse Channel 16 for radio checks.

question: Demonstrate how to manage a language barrier by speaking slowly and using simple vocabulary.
gold_answer: Slow down slightly, use short SMCP phrases, avoid idioms and slang, spell difficult names phonetically, and use digit-by-digit for numbers. Break complex requests into single-idea transmissions and use readbacks: "THIS IS (vessel), I UNDERSTAND BERTH C SEVEN, I SAY AGAIN, BERTH C SEVEN, CORRECT? OVER." If misunderstanding persists, request a shift to English-speaking staff or the coastguard, who typically has English fluency.
answer: 1. speak slowly. 2. use simple vocabulary. Outcome: effective communication despite language barriers. Warning: avoid complex phrases that may be misunderstood.

question: Perform a routine call to a bridge operator to request an opening at a specific time.
gold_answer: On the bridge's dedicated channel: "(Bridge name), THIS IS (Vessel) x3, OVER." On reply: "(Bridge), THIS IS (Vessel), SAILING YACHT, MAST HEIGHT (…) METRES, POSITION (…), REQUEST OPENING AT ONE FOUR THREE ZERO UTC, OVER." On confirmation readback: "THIS IS (Vessel), OPENING CONFIRMED FOR ONE FOUR THREE ZERO UTC, WILL HOLD SOUTH OF BRIDGE, THANK YOU, OUT."
answer: 1. perform a routine call. Outcome: successful communication with the bridge operator regarding the vessel's status and requests. Warning: ensure all safety equipment is operational before departure.

question: Show how to close the conversation correctly with the other station using appropriate pro-words.
gold_answer: After the substantive exchange is complete: "(other station), THIS IS (own vessel), STANDING BY ON CHANNEL (channel), OUT." Or if returning to normal watch: "...RETURNING TO CHANNEL ONE-SIX, THIS IS (own vessel), OUT." This signals no reply expected, states which channel you now monitor, and confirms your vessel identity. Log the time and outcome.
expected_points: state which channel you now monitor
answer: 1. say 'over' when you expect a reply. 2. say 'out' when you do not expect a reply. Outcome: clear communication of your intention regarding the conversation. Warning: saying 'over' does not necessarily mean you expect a reply.

question: Demonstrate calling a nearby yacht to coordinate rafting alongside at anchor.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: 3-3 identification, shift to an intership channel (e.g. Ch 72). On the working channel: "(other yacht), THIS IS (own vessel), REQUEST PERMISSION TO RAFT ALONGSIDE, WE ARE APPROACHING FROM NORTH-WEST, WILL COME PORT SIDE ALONGSIDE YOUR STARBOARD, POB (…), OVER." Await confirmation and coordinate approach and fender arrangement. Close with OUT.
expected_points: Ch 16 initial contact, shift to Ch 72
coordinate fenders and close with OUT
answer: 1. call the yacht on Channel 69. Outcome: successful communication with the yacht regarding rafting arrangements. Warning: ensure safety during transfer operations.

question: Perform a role-play where a mis-heard instruction is clarified using "SAY AGAIN" and phonetic spelling.
gold_answer: If the harbour master says "BERTH BAKER SEVEN" and it is unclear: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel), SAY AGAIN THE BERTH DESIGNATION, OVER." Harbour master responds: "THIS IS (HARBOUR), BERTH BAKER SEVEN, I SPELL BRAVO-ALFA-KILO-ECHO-ROMEO, SEVEN, OVER." Readback: "THIS IS (Vessel), BERTH BAKER SEVEN, I SPELL BRAVO-ALFA-KILO-ECHO-ROMEO, SEVEN, OVER." Harbour master confirms.
expected_points: use SAY AGAIN to request repetition
harbour master uses I SPELL with phonetic
answer: 1. say again. 2. spell the word or phrase clearly. Outcome: clarification of the mis-heard instruction. Warning: ensure clarity in communication to avoid confusion.

question: Show how to refuse an unsafe request from another vessel politely over VHF.
gold_answer: Use standard SMCP: "(other vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), NEGATIVE — I AM UNABLE TO (specific action) DUE TO (reason, e.g. draught limitations, sea state), REGRET NO ASSISTANCE POSSIBLE, OVER." Keep the refusal factual and brief, without judgement. If safety is genuinely at risk (e.g. request would put your vessel in danger), state that clearly so MRCC understands.
answer: 1. say 'No' three times. 2. say 'Stand by on VHF Channel ...'. Outcome: the other vessel understands that the request is refused and remains in standby mode. Warning: do not agree to requests that compromise safety.

question: Demonstrate the use of low power for local routine communications in a marina.
gold_answer: Press H/L to select LOW (1 W) before transmitting inside a marina or at short range. Confirm the display shows LO. Make the call as normal — a marina berthing exchange, a courtesy call to another yacht. Return to high power (25 W) once leaving the marina area or before making a coast station or distress call. Low power reduces both interference and battery drain.
expected_points: press H/L to select LOW (1 W)
use in marina or short range
return to high (25 W) offshore or for distress
answer: 1. use low power for local routine communications. Outcome: reduced interference with other vessels. Warning: high power should be used only when necessary.

question: Perform a routine call to request updated depth information from harbour control.
gold_answer: On port control channel: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel), REQUEST LATEST DEPTH AT (specific area, e.g. NORTH ENTRANCE) FOR VESSEL TWO METRES DRAUGHT, OVER." Harbour control replies with the current depth (chart datum + tidal height) and any dredge or spoil information. Readback and confirm. Log the depth and time received.
answer: 1. perform a routine call. Outcome: updated depth information is received from harbour control. Warning: ensure the vessel is clear of the fairway before anchoring.

question: Show how to handle simultaneous routine calls by instructing one caller to "STANDBY".
gold_answer: Answer each caller in turn on Ch 16 or the working channel: "(caller A), THIS IS (own vessel), STANDBY, OVER." Then answer caller B fully. Once done: "(caller A), THIS IS (own vessel), OVER." Handle in priority order (safety-related first), and if a wait exceeds a minute or two, use "STANDBY OUT" to free the channel.
expected_points: STANDBY OUT if wait exceeds 1–2 minutes
answer: 1. switch to Channel 68. Outcome: successful communication with the coast radio station. Warning: do not interrupt a conversation in progress.

question: Demonstrate logging an important routine communication (e.g., pilotage advice).
gold_answer: In the log record: UTC time, channel used, station name (e.g. Solent VTS), a factual summary of the pilotage advice (recommended course, holding position, tidal window), any instruction to switch channel, and confirmation given (readback). This creates a durable record that supports subsequent decisions and any incident review.
answer: 1. log important routine communications. Outcome: clear record of communications regarding pilotage advice and navigation status. Warning: ensure all communications are logged to avoid confusion.

question: Perform a short routine call with minimal words but full clarity, demonstrating concise communication.
gold_answer: Example: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel), TWO MINUTES OUT, LOCK ONE, PERMISSION TO ENTER, OVER." On reply: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel), ROGER, LOCK ONE, OUT." Only essential information — identity, position/timing, request — is included, and the exchange is closed cleanly. This is the SMCP ideal for routine calls.
expected_points: state single action (permission to enter Lock 1)
ROGER + station and OUT to close
answer: 1. perform a short routine call. Outcome: effective communication with the coast radio station. Warning: ensure clarity in communication to avoid misunderstandings.

question: Show how to re-establish contact with a station after a temporary radio or power failure.
gold_answer: After power is restored, verify the radio has booted normally, GPS position and MMSI are correct, and Ch 16 (or the working channel) is set. Then call the station: "(station), THIS IS (own vessel), FOLLOWING TEMPORARY LOSS OF COMMUNICATION, NOW BACK IN CONTACT, POSITION (…), OVER." Apologise briefly, confirm any previously agreed instructions (berth, ETA), and resume the exchange.
answer: 1. re-establish contact with the station. Outcome: successful communication is restored. Warning: ensure all communications are clear and concise.

question: Demonstrate using a handheld radio to coordinate mooring lines with crew while also communicating with harbour staff on the fixed radio.
gold_answer: Use the handheld on a low-power intership channel (e.g. Ch 72) to talk to the crew forward: "BOW LINE ON, WAITING FOR SPRING." Simultaneously the fixed radio remains on the harbour control channel for berthing instructions. Assign a crew member with SRC to monitor Ch 16 on the fixed set if you are focused on manoeuvring. Keep messages short and structured on both radios.
expected_points: handheld on intership channel (e.g. Ch 72), low power
fixed radio on harbour control channel
Ch 16 watch maintained by SRC-qualified crew
answer: 1. use 'OVER' when you have finished speaking and expect a reply. 2. use 'OUT' when you have finished speaking and do not expect a reply. 3. say 'THIS IS' followed by the name of your vessel. 4. say 'CALL SIGN' if you do not know the other station's identity. Outcome: effective communication during port operations. Warning: do not interrupt a conversation in progress.

question: Demonstrate programming the ship's MMSI into the DSC unit (or explain and show on simulator menu).
gold_answer: On the DSC menu open PROGRAM MMSI (usually inside SETUP). Enter the nine-digit MMSI issued by the national administration and confirm with ENTER. Most radios require the MMSI to be entered twice for confirmation and, once saved, lock the MMSI so it can only be changed by manufacturer reset. Verify the stored MMSI on the STATION ID screen. Never invent an MMSI or enter another vessel's.
expected_points: enter nine-digit MMSI issued by administration
answer: 1. program the ship's MMSI into the DSC unit. Outcome: successful communication with other vessels using DSC. Warning: ensure the MMSI is programmed correctly to avoid communication failures.

question: Show how to send a DSC individual routine call to a specified MMSI and then speak on the working channel.
gold_answer: Open DSC → INDIVIDUAL CALL → ROUTINE. Enter target MMSI, select working channel (e.g. Ch 72), press SEND. On acceptance both radios auto-switch. Then: "(target vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL SEVEN TWO, OVER." Proceed with substantive traffic; close with OUT and both return to Ch 16 watch afterwards.
expected_points: enter target MMSI and working channel
close with OUT and return to Ch 16
answer: 1. send a DSC individual routine call. Outcome: the called station receives the DSC call and acknowledges it. Warning: ensure the MMSI is correct before sending the call.

question: Demonstrate sending a DSC all-ships safety call (on simulator only).
gold_answer: On the simulator open DSC → ALL SHIPS → SAFETY. Confirm GPS position, select follow-up channel (typically Ch 16), and press SEND. The simulator transmits the safety alert on Ch 70 with own MMSI, position and safety category, then switches to Ch 16 for the voice SÉCURITÉ message. Follow up immediately with the voice SÉCURITÉ.
expected_points: confirm GPS position and follow-up channel
transmits on Ch 70 with safety category
answer: 1. send an all-ships safety call using DSC. Outcome: all ships in the vicinity receive the safety message. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is correct before sending the call.

question: Show how to send a DSC urgency alert and then follow with the appropriate voice call.
gold_answer: Open DSC → ALL SHIPS → URGENCY (or INDIVIDUAL for a specific coast station). Confirm GPS position, select Ch 16 as voice follow-up channel, press SEND. The radio transmits on Ch 70 with urgency category, then auto-switches to Ch 16. Immediately transmit the voice PAN PAN with all standard elements. Log the exchange.
expected_points: confirm GPS position and follow-up channel
answer: 1. send a DSC urgency alert. Outcome: the coast station receives the urgency alert. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is correct before sending the urgency alert.

question: Demonstrate reading and interpreting a received DSC distress alert on the display.
gold_answer: On alarm, silence with ALARM CANCEL and read the display: sender's MMSI, nature of distress (or UNDESIGNATED), position (lat/long), UTC time of position, and follow-up channel. Note MID (first 3 digits of MMSI) for flag state. Switch to Ch 16 and listen for the voice MAYDAY and coast station acknowledgement. Log all details.
expected_points: note MMSI, nature, position, time, channel
answer: 1. read the distress alert. Outcome: confirmation of receipt of the distress alert. Warning: failure to confirm receipt may delay rescue operations.

question: Show how to cancel a routine DSC call before it is transmitted.
gold_answer: During the compose/preview step press ESC or CANCEL to abort. If SEND has been pressed but the radio is still in the short pre-transmission delay, press CANCEL again — many sets will still block the transmission. Once transmitted, the call cannot be recalled; if incorrect, follow up with a corrective INDIVIDUAL call to the same target using DSC or voice.
expected_points: confirm the abort on the display
answer: 1. press the PTT button. 2. wait for a response. Outcome: the DSC call is successfully transmitted. Warning: ensure the DSC call is not transmitted if cancelled.

question: Demonstrate how to set up and send a DSC group call to a pre-defined group MMSI.
gold_answer: Open DSC → GROUP CALL, select the pre-programmed group MMSI (nine-digit starting with a leading zero, e.g. 023201234), choose the working channel, and press SEND. All radios with that group MMSI programmed will alert simultaneously. Follow up on the working channel with the group broadcast (e.g. rendezvous point or muster instruction).
expected_points: group MMSI starts with leading zero
voice follow-up on the working channel
answer: 1. set up a DSC call. Outcome: successful establishment of communication with the called station. Warning: ensure the MMSI is correctly programmed in the MFD.

question: Show how to verify GPS position data on the DSC radio and update it manually if necessary.
gold_answer: Check the position display: lat/long and UTC time should be current, no NO GPS warning. If GPS is unavailable, open MANUAL POSITION, enter lat/long (with hemispheres) and UTC time, and save. Display now shows MAN or USER indicator. Update the manual position every few minutes while GPS is unavailable, so any subsequent DSC distress alert has an accurate position.
expected_points: check position display and NO GPS warning
enter lat/long with hemispheres and UTC
update every few minutes while GPS is lost
answer: 1. verify GPS position data. 2. update position manually if GPS is not available. Outcome: accurate position information is communicated effectively. Warning: GPS may be unavailable in certain locations.

question: Demonstrate accessing the DSC call log and reviewing stored incoming alerts.
gold_answer: Open DSC → LOG → RECEIVED (or filter by DISTRESS / URGENCY / SAFETY / ROUTINE). Scroll to individual entries and press ENTER to view: MMSI, category, UTC time, position, follow-up channel. This is useful for reviewing missed alerts or reconstructing events. Some sets separate received and transmitted logs; check both.
expected_points: view MMSI, category, time, position, channel
check both received and transmitted logs
answer: 1. access the DSC call log. 2. review the call log entries. Outcome: successful communication with other vessels or shore stations. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is correctly programmed to avoid communication failures.

question: Show how to respond to a DSC routine call directed at your vessel.
gold_answer: When the DSC alerts, note the caller's MMSI and proposed channel on the display. Press ACCEPT / ACK — the radio switches automatically to the proposed channel. Reply by voice: "(caller), THIS IS (own vessel), CHANNEL (…), OVER." Proceed with the substantive exchange. If the channel is unsuitable, press REJECT and call the caller manually with an alternative.
expected_points: read caller MMSI and proposed channel
REJECT and manual call if channel unsuitable
answer: 1. respond to the DSC routine call. Outcome: successful communication with the coast radio station. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is correctly programmed in the DSC controller.

question: Demonstrate the correct sequence after receiving a DSC distress alert (voice follow-up, logging, standby).
gold_answer: 1. Silence alarm; note MMSI, nature, position, time. 2. Switch to Ch 16 (usually automatic). 3. Wait ~5 minutes in Sea Area A1 for the coast station to acknowledge — do not talk over. 4. If no coast station response and you can help, transmit acknowledgement and offer of assistance on Ch 16. 5. Log everything: time, MMSI, nature, position, coast station response, actions taken. Maintain listening watch until MRCC clears the incident.
expected_points: wait ~5 min for coast station in Sea Area A1
offer assistance only if no coast station responds
answer: 1. switch to voice communication. Outcome: effective communication during a distress situation. Warning: do not interrupt the distress traffic unless in charge of a lifeboat station.

question: Show how to mute and un-mute DSC alarms while still maintaining awareness.
gold_answer: When an alarm sounds, press ALARM CANCEL or SILENCE to mute the tone for the current alert while keeping the DSC watch active on Ch 70. Address the alert (read details, take action), then confirm the alarm system is fully re-enabled. Do not globally disable DSC alarms — this defeats the purpose of GMDSS watchkeeping.
expected_points: ALARM CANCEL / SILENCE for current alert
answer: 1. Mute the DSC alarm. 2. Un-mute the DSC alarm. Outcome: The DSC alarm is silenced temporarily. Warning: Do not press the red cross button during an emergency call.

question: Demonstrate storing a new MMSI in the DSC directory for frequent contacts.
gold_answer: Open DSC → DIRECTORY → NEW ENTRY. Enter the MMSI (verify with the vessel's owner or from the MMSI database), and give it a memorable label (e.g. "COASTGUARD SOLENT" or "FLOTILLA LEAD"). Save. Future INDIVIDUAL or GROUP calls can then be launched by selecting the name rather than typing the MMSI, reducing errors.
expected_points: future calls select by name to reduce errors
answer: 1. store a new MMSI in the DSC directory. Outcome: improved communication efficiency with frequent contacts. Warning: ensure the MMSI is active before using it.

question: Show how to modify or delete an incorrect MMSI entry from the directory.
gold_answer: Open DSC → DIRECTORY, select the entry to modify, press EDIT, change the MMSI or label, and save. To delete, select the entry and choose DELETE (some sets require confirmation). Verify the change and test with an INDIVIDUAL call to the corrected MMSI where practical. Keep the directory up to date so calls do not go to the wrong vessel.
expected_points: EDIT to change, DELETE to remove
answer: 1. modify or delete an incorrect MMSI entry. Outcome: updated information is communicated effectively. Warning: ensure all entries are current and accurate.

question: Demonstrate how to simulate a DSC test call and check that it is successful (simulator/training mode).
gold_answer: On the simulator or training mode, open DSC → TEST CALL, enter a coast station MMSI that supports automatic DSC test replies, and press SEND. Wait for the automated acknowledgement to appear in the log with the coast station's MMSI. Log the test date, time and result. In real operations, only send DSC test calls to stations that offer this service.
expected_points: target MMSI of coast station supporting test
log test date, time and result
answer: 1. switch the transmitter into working mode. Outcome: the DSC engine is activated and ready for communication. Warning: do not press the PTT button during a DSC call.

question: Show how to change the category of a DSC call (routine, safety, urgency) before sending.
gold_answer: During DSC call setup, before pressing SEND, use the up/down keys or a soft key to select the desired category — ROUTINE for normal traffic, SAFETY (SÉCURITÉ equivalent), URGENCY (PAN PAN equivalent) or DISTRESS for MAYDAY. The category determines the alarm behaviour on the receiving side and the channel priority. Verify the category on the display before SEND.
expected_points: change category during setup, before SEND
answer: 1. select Routine, Safety, or Urgency. Outcome: the call is transmitted with the selected category. Warning: ensure the MMSI number is valid and entered.

question: Demonstrate troubleshooting steps when DSC fails to send (e.g., no GPS, antenna/VSWR issues explained).
gold_answer: Check the display for error messages: NO GPS (enter manual position), NO MMSI (radio not configured), NO ACK (target station out of range or off), high VSWR / antenna warning (inspect antenna, coax, connectors). Verify supply voltage; low voltage may cause resets. Test on a working channel with a radio check. Log the fault and consult the manual or a marine electrician if unresolved.
expected_points: antenna/VSWR issues → inspect antenna and coax
low voltage → check battery and fuses
answer: 1. check GPS connection. 2. verify antenna connection. 3. confirm VHF antenna voltage standing wave ratio. Outcome: successful DSC call transmission. Warning: ensure GPS is connected for position reporting.

question: Show how to integrate DSC operation into a broader emergency drill involving EPIRB and AIS.
gold_answer: In the drill: (1) send a DSC distress alert on the simulator; (2) transmit voice MAYDAY on Ch 16; (3) simulate activating the EPIRB (using the built-in test only, never live); (4) confirm AIS-SART or AIS position transmission if fitted; (5) verify each system's watch and log entries. Debrief the crew on how the three systems complement each other: DSC alerts near vessels, EPIRB gives satellite backup, AIS-SART marks the raft.
answer: 1. perform an emergency drill. Outcome: crew members are familiar with emergency procedures. Warning: ensure all life-saving appliances are operational before departure.

question: Demonstrate maintaining a DSC watch while simultaneously using voice channels.
gold_answer: The DSC watch on Ch 70 is automatic and independent of voice channel selection — the radio scans Ch 70 continuously. While transmitting or receiving voice on Ch 16 or any working channel, the DSC watch remains active in the background. Confirm the DSC watch indicator is displayed. Never disable the DSC watch except when the vessel is in port with the radio off.
expected_points: DSC watch on Ch 70 is automatic
runs in the background during voice traffic
confirm DSC watch indicator on display
never disable except when in port and radio off
answer: DSC stands for Digital Selective Calling. Channel 16 is the primary distress channel for DSC. Outcome: effective communication during emergencies. Warning: DSC is not a substitute for traditional voice hailing.

question: Perform a brief explanation to the examiner of how DSC operations are tested in international SRC exams.
gold_answer: SRC exam DSC testing typically requires the candidate to demonstrate on a simulator: sending a DSC distress alert with correct nature and position, cancelling a false alert (DSC cancel + voice cancellation on Ch 16), initiating an INDIVIDUAL DSC routine call to a specified MMSI, interpreting a received DSC distress alert, and identifying the correct actions in Sea Area A1 (wait for coast station acknowledgement, log all details).
expected_points: send DSC distress with correct nature and position
INDIVIDUAL routine call to a specified MMSI
interpret a received DSC distress alert
answer: DSC stands for Digital Selective Calling. Channel 16 is used for distress calls. Outcome: successful communication during emergencies. Warning: Channel 16 must be used only for distress calls.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate testing an EPIRB using the manufacturer's test function without triggering a real alert.
gold_answer: Locate the EPIRB's TEST button (often a separate small button or a press-and-hold sequence). Press as per manufacturer's instructions (typically 1-second press). Observe the test LED sequence and audible beep confirming battery, GPS lock (on GPS-equipped units) and self-test pass. Do NOT hold the button long enough to trigger a real 406 MHz transmission. Log the test date and result.
expected_points: observe test LED and audible sequence
do NOT trigger real 406 MHz transmission
answer: 1. test the EPIRB. Outcome: confirmation that the EPIRB is operational. Warning: do not test the EPIRB in port or at sea unless instructed by the Coastguard.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to read and interpret the EPIRB label (MMSI/hex ID, expiry dates, registration info).
gold_answer: On the EPIRB label read: unique 15-character HEX ID (Cospas-Sarsat identity), MMSI (if configured), battery expiry date, hydrostatic release unit (HRU) expiry date, manufacturer, model, country code and registration reference. Verify the HEX ID matches your registration record. Expiry dates should be checked pre-departure and replaced when due — an out-of-date battery may fail during a real activation.
expected_points: match HEX ID to registration record
answer: 1. check the validity of the EPIRB/PLB. Outcome: confirmation of the operational status of the EPIRB/PLB. Warning: ensure the EPIRB/PLB is operational before deployment.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate checking the hydrostatic release unit (if fitted) for expiry date and condition.
gold_answer: Locate the HRU (hydrostatic release unit) attached to the EPIRB bracket. Read the expiry date stamped on the HRU housing — typically 2 years from manufacture. Inspect for corrosion, physical damage or salt build-up. If expiry is within 6 months or the HRU shows visible damage, replace it. Log the inspection and any replacement.
answer: 1. check the hydrostatic release unit (if fitted). Outcome: confirmation of operational readiness regarding lifeboat equipment. Warning: ensure all lifeboats/liferafts are operational.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to test a SART or AIS-SART in test mode according to instructions.
gold_answer: Remove the SART from its bracket. Follow the manufacturer's test procedure — typically press and hold the TEST button until the test LEDs sequence and an audible tone confirms success. For AIS-SART, some units display a TEST message. The test is normally brief (10–20 seconds) and does not transmit a real distress signal. Log the test date and result and return the unit to its bracket.
expected_points: test does not transmit real distress
log date and result, return to bracket
answer: 1. switch the DSC alert acknowledgement function on/off. 2. press the red button for 5 seconds. Outcome: successful testing of the SART or AIS-SART. Warning: ensure the SART is switched off after testing.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to ensure NAVTEX or equivalent MSI receiver is set to relevant message categories and stations.
gold_answer: On the NAVTEX receiver open SETUP → STATIONS and select the stations that cover the intended sea area (identified by letter A–X). Then in CATEGORIES enable the relevant message categories — typically A (navigational warnings), B (meteorological), D (SAR), and disable those you don't need. Verify by observing incoming messages. Reconfigure when moving into a new sea area.
expected_points: CATEGORIES: enable A, B, D minimum
answer: 1. ensure NAVTEX or equivalent MSI receiver is set to relevant message categories and stations. Outcome: timely receipt of MSI. Warning: ensure receiver is operational for safety.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to acknowledge a received NAVTEX safety message on the display and relate its contents.
gold_answer: NAVTEX messages appear on the display with station letter, category letter, message number and time. To "acknowledge", press READ or open the message; on many units this marks it as read and removes it from the unread queue. Read the content, note any effect on the passage plan, log a summary and (if useful) print the message. NAVTEX itself does not require you to transmit any acknowledgement.
expected_points: log summary and print if useful
answer: 1. Acknowledge receipt of the safety message. Outcome: The safety message is confirmed received by the mariner. Warning: Failure to acknowledge may result in safety hazards.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to check that GMDSS batteries are in good condition and properly charged (explanation and checks).
gold_answer: Check each battery-powered GMDSS item (portable VHF, EPIRB, PLB, SART, AIS-SART): battery expiry date on the label, no swelling or corrosion, terminal contacts clean. Where possible use the manufacturer's TEST function to confirm capacity. For rechargeable batteries verify a full charge and store on the charger. Log the check date. Replace any battery within 6 months of expiry.
expected_points: check expiry date on each battery
replace any battery within 6 months of expiry
answer: 1. check the condition of GMDSS batteries. 2. ensure batteries are charged. Outcome: confirmation that the GMDSS equipment is operational. Warning: GMDSS equipment must be operational at all times.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to store EPIRB and SART correctly for rapid deployment.
gold_answer: Stow the EPIRB in its dedicated bracket in an accessible location (usually near a companionway or on deck), with HRU armed. Stow SART/AIS-SART in bracket close to the liferaft or grab bag, quickly reachable. Both must be free of any covers that would prevent hydrostatic activation or manual removal. Include their location in the safety brief so any crew can retrieve them.
expected_points: EPIRB in dedicated bracket, HRU armed
SART near liferaft or grab bag
answer: 1. store EPIRB and/or SART in a safe place. Outcome: increased safety during emergencies. Warning: ensure EPIRB and/or SART is accessible for immediate use.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to launch a SART from its bracket in a simulated emergency.
gold_answer: Release the SART from its bracket (typically by rotating a lock or pressing a release). Extend the telescoping antenna to its full height. Activate per manufacturer's instructions (usually a switch or a press-and-hold). Hold as high as possible in the liferaft — a broomstick or paddle extension is recommended for maximum range. Once activated, do not switch off until rescue arrives or the battery expires.
expected_points: hold as high as possible in liferaft
do not switch off until rescue or battery expires
answer: 1. check the SART for expiry date. 2. confirm the SART is operational. Outcome: confirmation that the EPIRB/SART is operational and ready for use. Warning: ensure the EPIRB/SART has sufficient battery life.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to integrate use of EPIRB and VHF DSC distress alert in an abandon-ship drill.
gold_answer: In the drill sequence: (1) send DSC distress alert with nature ABANDONING SHIP; (2) transmit voice MAYDAY on Ch 16 stating intention; (3) manually activate EPIRB (simulate; do NOT hold long enough for a real transmission); (4) take EPIRB, handheld VHF, SART and grab bag into the liferaft; (5) once in the raft, monitor Ch 16 on handheld and keep SART active. Debrief on sequence and roles.
expected_points: DSC distress with ABANDONING SHIP nature
take EPIRB, handheld VHF, SART, grab bag
monitor Ch 16 on handheld from raft
answer: 1. call MAYDAY on DSC. Outcome: successful distress communication with rescue services. Warning: ensure all safety equipment is operational before departure.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to interpret a NAVTEX message giving a navigational warning.
gold_answer: Read the header: station letter, category (A = navigational warning), message number and time. Read the body for area affected, position, description of the hazard, effect on shipping and any recommended action or route. Plot the hazard on the chart, note whether it affects the current or intended passage, and log a summary with actions taken (course change, extra watch).
expected_points: read header: station, category A, number, time
description of hazard and effect on shipping
log summary and any action taken
answer: 1. listen to NAVTEX broadcasts. Outcome: improved situational awareness regarding navigational warnings and meteorological information. Warning: NAVTEX messages may be delayed by up to 5 hours.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to verify the correct registration of an EPIRB with national authorities (explained, with sample data).
gold_answer: Contact the national beacon registry (e.g. UK: The Beacon Registry, HM Coastguard; NL: Kustwacht Nederland) with the beacon's HEX ID. Verify that the registered owner, vessel details, 24/7 emergency contacts and beacon type match. Update any changes (ownership, contact numbers) immediately. Registration is normally free and can be checked online. An unregistered beacon delays SAR response significantly.
answer: 1. register your EPIRB with HM Coastguard. Outcome: improved safety at sea through effective communication and tracking. Warning: failure to register may result in fines or penalties.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to silence an accidentally activated EPIRB and report the false alert to authorities (simulated).
gold_answer: Turn the EPIRB switch back to OFF or return to its bracket according to model instructions. Immediately call the coastguard on Ch 16 or by phone: "(COASTGUARD), THIS IS (vessel), CANCEL FALSE EPIRB ALERT, HEX ID (…), TIME OF ACTIVATION (…), CAUSE (inadvertent), NO ASSISTANCE REQUIRED, OVER." Provide vessel details for cross-reference. Log the event. Confirm cancellation with the coastguard before ending contact.
expected_points: switch EPIRB off or return to bracket
call coastguard on Ch 16 or by phone
state CANCEL FALSE EPIRB ALERT with HEX ID
give time and cause of activation
answer: 1. silence the EPIRB. Outcome: the EPIRB is silenced and no further distress alerts are sent. Warning: accidental activation of an EPIRB can lead to false distress alerts.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to read off the battery expiry date on EPIRB and SART and record it in the log.
gold_answer: Locate the battery expiry label on the EPIRB (typically front or side panel) and on the SART (usually beside the manufacturer's label). Read the month and year (e.g. "BATTERY EXPIRES 08/2029"). Record both dates in the vessel's safety-equipment log, along with the inspection date. Set a calendar reminder for at least 6 months before each expiry so replacement can be arranged.
expected_points: locate expiry label on EPIRB and SART
set calendar reminder 6 months before expiry
answer: 1. check the battery expiry date on EPIRB/SART. 2. record the expiry date in the log. Outcome: confirmation of the operational status of EPIRB/SART. Warning: ensure the EPIRB/SART is operational before departure.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to secure GMDSS equipment so that it remains usable after heavy weather.
gold_answer: Ensure EPIRB is firmly in its bracket with HRU armed but not obstructed. Store SART in a padded holder or bracket. Handheld VHF should be in a padded case, secured against sudden motion, in a location protected from spray. Grab bag containing spare batteries, PLBs and flares should be securely stowed near the companionway, waterproof and accessible with one hand. Do a pre-departure check on all fastenings.
expected_points: EPIRB firmly bracketed, HRU not obstructed
handheld VHF in padded case, protected from spray
answer: 1. secure all portable equipment. Outcome: equipment is protected from movement during heavy weather. Warning: ensure all equipment is secured to avoid loss or damage.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to incorporate GMDSS systems checks into a pre-voyage checklist.
gold_answer: Add to the pre-voyage checklist: (1) fixed VHF/DSC boot self-test, GPS position, correct MMSI; (2) handheld VHF battery and antenna; (3) EPIRB self-test and HRU condition; (4) SART self-test; (5) NAVTEX / MSI receiver on and receiving; (6) safety-equipment log up to date. Sign off each item before departure. This ensures that any pre-existing fault is caught in port, not at sea.
answer: 1. check the GMDSS equipment. Outcome: confirmation that all required equipment is operational. Warning: ensure all equipment is operational before departure.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate how to retrieve and interpret AIS SAR target information relevant to a distress.
gold_answer: On the AIS display filter for SAR targets (typically shown as SAR aircraft symbol or SAR-SART marker). Select the target to view its MMSI, name, position, course, speed and CPA/TCPA. In a distress this shows where SAR units are and their ETA to the casualty. If the AIS is integrated with the VHF, an INDIVIDUAL DSC call can be initiated directly to the SAR unit's MMSI. Log the interaction.
expected_points: view MMSI, name, position, course, speed
integrated VHF can DSC-call the SAR unit
answer: 1. request AIS information. Outcome: improved situational awareness regarding nearby vessels. Warning: ensure all communications are clear and concise.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to combine voice, DSC, and GMDSS equipment in a coordinated SAR training scenario.
gold_answer: In the training scenario the on-scene actions run in parallel: DSC alert on the simulator, voice MAYDAY on Ch 16, EPIRB self-test, SART/AIS-SART in test mode, handheld VHF for the liferaft, and MRCC coordination on Ch 67 or working channel. One crew member is designated for each system so activities do not conflict. Debrief at the end to align system knowledge across the crew.
expected_points: DSC + voice MAYDAY + EPIRB + SART/AIS-SART + handheld
parallel actions with dedicated crew role each
MRCC coordination on a working channel
test modes only — no live transmissions
answer: 1. combine voice, DSC, and GMDSS equipment. Outcome: effective communication during search-and-rescue operations. Warning: ensure all equipment is operational before departure.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Demonstrate explaining to crew the basic functions of EPIRB and SART in a safety briefing.
gold_answer: Explain: "The EPIRB is our satellite-based distress beacon; when we activate it (or if it floats free with the HRU), it tells the Cospas-Sarsat satellites and MRCC where we are. The SART is a small radar responder we take into the liferaft; it makes us visible to any nearby SAR radar as a distinctive twelve-dot line. Location of each is here (show the bracket) and this is the manual activation button." Keep it under 3 minutes and end with a hands-on point-and-name test.
expected_points: EPIRB = satellite distress beacon via Cospas-Sarsat
answer: 1. ensure all lifejackets are available and inspected. 2. confirm EPIRB/SART is operational. 3. check if crew can swim. Outcome: crew is aware of their equipment and safety procedures. Warning: ensure all lifejackets are available before departure.

section_title: Operational Procedures for the GMDSS Components
question: Show how to log all GMDSS system tests and maintenance actions in a structured way.
gold_answer: Maintain a GMDSS log with columns: date, system (VHF/DSC, EPIRB, SART, handheld, NAVTEX, AIS), test performed, result (pass/fail), any action taken, and signature of tester. Test intervals: weekly DSC check, monthly EPIRB and SART self-test, annual professional service. Keep the log with the ship station licence documents. This structured record supports insurance, coastguard audits and future incident reviews.
expected_points: date, system, test, result, action, signature
test intervals: weekly DSC, monthly EPIRB/SART
answer: 1. log all DSC system tests and maintenance actions. Outcome: comprehensive documentation of communication system status. Warning: ensure all equipment is operational before departure.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Conduct a short radio conversation using correct "THIS IS", "OVER", and "OUT".
gold_answer: Example: "(Marina), (Marina), (Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), OVER." (Marina): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Marina), GO AHEAD, OVER." (Vessel): "(Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), REQUEST OVERNIGHT BERTH, ETA ONE SEVEN ZERO ZERO UTC, OVER." (Marina): "THIS IS (Marina), BERTH F THREE, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), BERTH F THREE, THANK YOU, OUT." Illustrates initial 3-3 identification, OVER between transmissions, THIS IS on continuations, and OUT to close.
expected_points: OUT to close with no reply expected
answer: Prowords enhance communication clarity in maritime radio operations. Outcome: improved communication efficiency during radio conversations. Warning: incorrect prowords may lead to misunderstandings.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate correcting a mistake mid-transmission using "CORRECTION".
gold_answer: Example: "THIS IS (Vessel), MY POSITION IS FIVE ZERO ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE WEST — CORRECTION, ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE EAST, OVER." The pro-word CORRECTION explicitly voids the previous statement and signals the corrected version to follow.
expected_points: then the corrected word or phrase
answer: 1. say 'CORRECTION'. Outcome: the listener receives the corrected information. Warning: do not say 'THIS IS WRONG' or 'REPEAT'.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to ask for repetition of a specific part of a message using "SAY AGAIN".
gold_answer: Options: "SAY AGAIN YOUR POSITION, OVER." "SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER 'PORT SIDE', OVER." "SAY AGAIN ALL BEFORE 'STARBOARD', OVER." "SAY AGAIN WORD BEFORE 'CHANNEL', OVER." Never use "repeat" — that is a military artillery pro-word. Structuring the request tells the other station exactly what to re-transmit and saves time.
answer: 1. say 'SAY AGAIN' if the message is not understood. Outcome: clarification of the message. Warning: do not repeat the entire message if only a part is unclear.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate placing another station on hold using "STANDBY" and then resuming communication.
gold_answer: Example: "(caller), THIS IS (own vessel), STANDBY, OVER." (Attend to the other task.) When ready to resume: "(caller), THIS IS (own vessel), OVER." (Caller): "(own vessel), THIS IS (caller), OVER." (Own vessel): "THIS IS (own vessel), CONTINUE WITH YOUR MESSAGE, OVER." STANDBY holds the channel; STANDBY OUT can be used to free the channel if the wait is longer.
expected_points: use STANDBY OUT if wait is longer
answer: 1. say 'OVER' when you have finished speaking. Outcome: the other party knows that the conversation is over. Warning: saying 'OVER' does not mean the other person should stop talking.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to acknowledge instructions clearly using "ROGER".
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Coastguard), REDUCE SPEED TO FIVE KNOTS, OVER." (Vessel): "(Coastguard), THIS IS (Vessel), ROGER, OVER." ROGER signals "received and understood" but implies no action commitment. If action is required and will be complied with, use WILCO instead. Do not combine as ROGER WILCO — it is redundant.
expected_points: does not imply action or agreement
answer: 1. repeat instructions. Outcome: the officer acknowledges the instructions and confirms readiness for the next station. Warning: ensure all instructions are acknowledged before proceeding.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate using "WILCO" correctly in response to an order.
gold_answer: Example: (Harbour Control): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Harbour), HOLD SOUTH OF NORTH ENTRANCE UNTIL FURTHER NOTICE, OVER." (Vessel): "(Harbour), THIS IS (Vessel), WILCO, OVER." WILCO ("WILL COMPLY") means received, understood and will carry out. Never combine with ROGER — WILCO already includes the meaning of ROGER.
expected_points: implies received, understood and will comply
use only when action will be taken
answer: 1. say 'WILCO' followed by the station name. Outcome: confirmation of receipt and compliance with the order. Warning: ensure clarity when communicating orders.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to use "BREAK" to separate parts of a message during a longer transmission.
gold_answer: Example MAYDAY: "MAYDAY (vessel), POSITION FIVE ZERO ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE NORTH, ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE WEST, BREAK, NATURE OF DISTRESS FIRE ON BOARD, BREAK, POB FIVE, ONE INJURED, BREAK, ABANDONING TO LIFERAFT, OVER." BREAK marks logical separation between position, nature, POB and situation so the listener can copy each section.
expected_points: BREAK marks logical separation within one transmission
used inside MAYDAY between position, nature, POB, situation
answer: 1. say 'BREAK' three times. Outcome: the other station knows that you have finished speaking and they can respond. Warning: do not say 'OVER' if you need a response.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate using "I SPELL" followed by phonetic spelling of a harbour name.
gold_answer: Example: "THIS IS (Vessel), DESTINATION SCHEVENINGEN, I SPELL SIERRA-CHARLIE-HOTEL-ECHO-VICTOR-ECHO-NOVEMBER-INDIA-NOVEMBER-GOLF-ECHO-NOVEMBER, SCHEVENINGEN, OVER." The plain word first tells the listener the pronunciation; I SPELL introduces the phonetic breakdown; the plain word after confirms the whole.
answer: 1. say 'OVER' after each statement. Outcome: clear communication with the other party. Warning: do not say 'OVER AND OUT'.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to use "ALL STATIONS" at the start of a broadcast message.
gold_answer: Example SÉCURITÉ: "SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, SÉCURITÉ, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, ALL STATIONS, THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), NAVIGATIONAL WARNING: (…), OUT." ALL STATIONS three times addresses every listener; it is used for MAYDAY, PAN PAN, SÉCURITÉ and general navigational broadcasts.
expected_points: used for MAYDAY, PAN PAN, SÉCURITÉ
followed by THIS IS + calling identity x3
answer: 1. use 'ALL STATIONS' at the start of a broadcast message. Outcome: all stations within range receive the message. Warning: do not use 'ALL STATIONS' unless broadcasting to a wide area.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate ending a call correctly without saying "OVER AND OUT".
gold_answer: Correct endings: "THIS IS (Vessel), OUT." or "THIS IS (Vessel), STANDING BY ON CHANNEL ONE SIX, OUT." "OVER AND OUT" is a Hollywood invention combining two contradictory pro-words. OVER expects a reply; OUT ends the conversation. Choose one — usually OUT for the final transmission.
expected_points: end with OUT for final transmission
optionally state which channel you now monitor
answer: 1. say 'OVER' when you have finished speaking. Outcome: the other party knows it is their turn to speak. Warning: do not say 'OVER AND OUT' together.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to handle overlapping transmissions by using appropriate phrases to re-establish order.
gold_answer: If two stations transmit simultaneously and cannot be understood, the controlling station may say: "STATIONS CALLING (own vessel name), THIS IS (own vessel), CALL ONE AT A TIME, OVER." Each station then calls in turn. If two stations both realise they were transmitting, both should release PTT immediately, wait a couple of seconds, and let the called station identify who to call first.
expected_points: controlling station says STATIONS CALLING (name), CALL ONE AT A TIME
each station then calls in turn
short wait to reset the channel
answer: 1. stop transmitting immediately. 2. wait for a short interval before continuing. 3. repeat the transmission after a short interval. Outcome: improved clarity in communication. Warning: do not interrupt another station while it is transmitting.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate a short routine call including at least five correct pro-words.
gold_answer: Example: "(Marina), (Marina), (Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), OVER." (Marina): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Marina), GO AHEAD, OVER." (Vessel): "(Marina), THIS IS (Vessel), REQUEST BERTH FOR ONE NIGHT, ETA ONE SIX ZERO ZERO UTC, OVER." (Marina): "THIS IS (Marina), BERTH BAKER FIVE, I SPELL BRAVO ALFA KILO ECHO ROMEO, FIVE, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), ROGER, BERTH BAKER FIVE, THANK YOU, OUT." Uses: THIS IS, OVER, ROGER, I SPELL, OUT.
answer: Prowords are standardized phrases for effective communication. Outcome: improved clarity in communication during emergencies. Warning: misuse of prowords may cause confusion.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to politely decline a request using clear, standard phraseology.
gold_answer: Example: "(other vessel), THIS IS (own vessel), NEGATIVE, UNABLE TO PROVIDE TOW DUE TO ADVERSE SEA STATE AND OWN VESSEL SAFETY, RECOMMEND YOU CONTACT COASTGUARD ON CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER." NEGATIVE is the standard refusal; providing a specific reason and a suggested alternative keeps the exchange helpful and factual.
expected_points: suggest an alternative (e.g. coastguard, other vessel)
answer: 1. say 'Over' after your last word. Outcome: the other party knows it is their turn to speak. Warning: do not say 'Over' until you have finished speaking.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate hearing a poorly transmitted message and requesting a repeat using standard words.
gold_answer: Example: "(other station), THIS IS (own vessel), YOUR SIGNAL IS UNREADABLE, SAY AGAIN YOUR ENTIRE MESSAGE, OVER." Or more specific: "YOUR SIGNAL IS BROKEN, SAY AGAIN ALL AFTER 'POSITION', OVER." Standard phraseology (SAY AGAIN, SIGNAL UNREADABLE / BROKEN) tells the other station exactly what is needed.
answer: 1. say again. 2. request a repeat. Outcome: clarification of the message is obtained. Warning: ensure clarity in communication to avoid misunderstandings.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to confirm understanding of a complex instruction by repeating it back ("readback").
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Coastguard), PROCEED TO POSITION FIVE ZERO ONE TWO NORTH ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE WEST, HOLD AT REDUCED SPEED, MONITOR CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER." (Vessel): "(Coastguard), THIS IS (Vessel), READBACK: PROCEED TO POSITION FIVE ZERO ONE TWO NORTH ZERO ZERO ONE FOUR FIVE WEST, HOLD AT REDUCED SPEED, MONITOR CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OVER." Coastguard confirms with ROGER.
expected_points: allows the sender to confirm accuracy
standard SMCP practice for complex instructions
answer: 1. confirm understanding of instructions. Outcome: clear communication regarding navigation and safety measures. Warning: failure to confirm instructions may lead to misunderstandings.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate using "AFFIRMATIVE" and "NEGATIVE" clearly instead of "YES" or "NO".
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Coastguard), CONFIRM YOU HAVE FIVE PERSONS ON BOARD, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), AFFIRMATIVE, POB FIVE, OVER." And: "(Vessel), CONFIRM YOU HAVE MEDICAL EMERGENCY, OVER." (Vessel): "NEGATIVE, NO MEDICAL EMERGENCY, OVER." These words are noise-resistant and unambiguous.
expected_points: preferred over YES / NO on radio
answer: 1. say 'AFFIRMATIVE' or 'NEGATIVE'. Outcome: clear communication regarding the response to the question. Warning: do not say 'YES' or 'NO' instead of 'AFFIRMATIVE' or 'NEGATIVE'.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to manage a handover of communication from one officer to another over the radio.
gold_answer: Example: "(Coastguard), THIS IS (Vessel), COMMUNICATIONS OFFICER HANDING OVER TO SKIPPER, STAND BY, OVER." On resumption: "(Coastguard), THIS IS (Vessel), SKIPPER NOW ON THE RADIO, OVER." Log the handover time and the identity of the new operator. Notify any coordinating station so they know who they are talking to. On short exchanges the same operator normally stays on the radio.
expected_points: identify the new operator on resumption
answer: 1. manage communication between officers. Outcome: effective communication during navigation and operations. Warning: ensure clear communication to avoid misunderstandings.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Demonstrate how to indicate the end of a broadcast message where no reply is expected.
gold_answer: For broadcasts (SÉCURITÉ, MAYDAY RELAY, MSI), end with OUT rather than OVER, since no direct reply from a specific station is expected. Example: "...VESSELS ADVISED KEEP CLEAR, THIS IS (Vessel), OUT." This tells all listeners the transmission is complete. If clarifications are invited on a working channel, mention it: "...CLARIFICATIONS ON CHANNEL SIX SEVEN, OUT."
expected_points: no reply from specific station expected
optionally invite clarifications on working channel
OVER would incorrectly imply awaited reply
answer: 1. say 'OVER' at the end of a message. Outcome: the other station knows that you have finished speaking and are waiting for a reply. Warning: do not say 'OVER AND OUT' unless expecting a reply.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Show how to phrase a message so that the "who, where, what" structure is clear and concise.
gold_answer: Example: "(HARBOUR), THIS IS (Vessel) [WHO], APPROACHING FROM SOUTH ENTRANCE [WHERE], REQUEST PERMISSION TO ENTER AND BERTH IN VISITOR AREA [WHAT], ETA ONE SIX ZERO ZERO UTC [WHEN], OVER." Each element is short and complete. This structure lets the harbour master respond in a single transmission with clearance and berth assignment.
expected_points: WHO – both station names and vessel identity
short and complete for a single-response reply
answer: 1. use the 'Who, Where, What' structure. Outcome: effective communication of information regarding the vessel's status. Warning: ensure clarity in communication to avoid misunderstandings.

section_title: Use of the Procedure Words and Phrases
question: Conduct a short multi-step scenario where proper use of procedure words prevents misunderstanding.
gold_answer: Scenario: berthing exchange in poor visibility. (Vessel): "(Harbour), (Harbour), (Harbour), THIS IS (Vessel), (Vessel), (Vessel), OVER." (Harbour): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Harbour), GO AHEAD, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), TWELVE METRES LOA, VISIBILITY ONE HUNDRED METRES, REQUEST GUIDANCE FOR BERTHING, OVER." (Harbour): "THIS IS (Harbour), PROCEED TO WAITING PONTOON, TURN STARBOARD AT NORTH CARDINAL, I SPELL WHISKEY PAPA, OVER." (Vessel): "READBACK: WAITING PONTOON, TURN STARBOARD AT NORTH CARDINAL WHISKEY PAPA, OVER." (Harbour): "ROGER, OUT." Use of THIS IS, OVER, I SPELL, READBACK, ROGER and OUT keeps this potentially hazardous exchange unambiguous.
answer: 1. use 'OVER' when you have finished speaking and expect a reply. 2. use 'OUT' when you have finished with everyone on the channel. Outcome: clear communication between vessels. Warning: do not say 'OVER AND OUT' together as it confuses people.

question: Spell the vessel's name on request using the phonetic alphabet.
gold_answer: Example for vessel PEGASUS: "THIS IS SAILING VESSEL PEGASUS, I SPELL PAPA-ECHO-GOLF-ALFA-SIERRA-UNIFORM-SIERRA, PEGASUS, OVER." The plain word first indicates pronunciation; I SPELL introduces the phonetic breakdown; the plain word after confirms the whole.
expected_points: include OVER or full station identification
answer: 1. spell the vessel's name on request. Outcome: clear communication of the vessel's name. Warning: do not use the phonetic alphabet unless requested.

question: Spell your own surname and first name using the phonetic alphabet.
gold_answer: Example surname SMITH, first name JOHN: "SURNAME SMITH, I SPELL SIERRA-MIKE-INDIA-TANGO-HOTEL, SMITH. FIRST NAME JOHN, I SPELL JULIETT-OSCAR-HOTEL-NOVEMBER, JOHN. OVER." Spelling both is essential in SAR to ensure hospitals, embassies and next-of-kin records are accurate.
expected_points: state plain surname and first name
answer: 1. spell your own surname and first name using the phonetic alphabet. Outcome: clear communication of names over VHF radio. Warning: do not use the phonetic alphabet for spelling numbers.

question: Spell the port of destination using phonetic letters.
gold_answer: Example destination BREST: "THIS IS (Vessel), DESTINATION BREST, I SPELL BRAVO-ROMEO-ECHO-SIERRA-TANGO, BREST, OVER." Especially important for ports whose names are not English (Brest, Calais, IJmuiden, Vigo) where non-native listeners could easily misread them.
expected_points: essential for foreign or non-English port names
answer: 1. spell the name of the vessel. Outcome: clear communication of vessel details. Warning: ensure phonetic spelling is used to avoid confusion.

question: Spell the MMSI "211450001" digit by digit using correct number pronunciation.
gold_answer: "MMSI TWO-ONE-ONE-FOWER-FIFE-ZERO-ZERO-ZERO-ONE." Digit by digit, with FOWER for 4, FIFE for 5, ZERO for 0. Speak clearly with a short pause between groups (e.g. after the first three MID digits). Do not read "211" as "two hundred and eleven" — digit-by-digit prevents confusion.
answer: Pronunciation: TWO WUN WUN FOUR FIFE Zero ONE. Outcome: successful communication of the MMSI number. Warning: ensure clarity in MMSI number transmission to avoid errors.

question: Spell a waypoint name (given by examiner) that is difficult to understand over radio.
gold_answer: Example waypoint TX3 (given by examiner): "WAYPOINT TX3, I SPELL TANGO-XRAY, THREE, TX3, OVER." For a longer name like GRAVELINES: "GRAVELINES, I SPELL GOLF-ROMEO-ALFA-VICTOR-ECHO-LIMA-INDIA-NOVEMBER-ECHO-SIERRA, GRAVELINES, OVER." Combine plain name, I SPELL, phonetic and readback for any name likely to be misheard.
answer: 1. spell the waypoint name clearly. Outcome: clear communication of the waypoint name. Warning: do not use phonetic alphabets for names.

question: Demonstrate reading back a spelled-out word from another station to confirm accurate reception.
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "MEDICAL CONDITION IS ANGINA, I SPELL ALFA-NOVEMBER-GOLF-INDIA-NOVEMBER-ALFA, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), READBACK ANGINA, I SPELL ALFA-NOVEMBER-GOLF-INDIA-NOVEMBER-ALFA, ANGINA, OVER." The coastguard then confirms with ROGER. Readback ensures both stations have identical wording of a critical term.
expected_points: I SPELL with same phonetic letters
await confirmation from the other station
answer: 1. spell out words clearly. Outcome: clear communication of complex terms or names. Warning: ensure clarity in spelling to avoid misunderstandings.

question: Spell the vessel's call sign combining letters and numbers.
gold_answer: Example call sign 2ABC5: "CALL SIGN TWO-ALFA-BRAVO-CHARLIE-FIVE" or fully phrased: "THIS IS (Vessel), CALL SIGN TWO, I SPELL ALFA-BRAVO-CHARLIE, FIVE, OVER." Each character is spoken separately, letters with phonetic words and digits with radiotelephony pronunciation. Do not try to read the call sign as a word.
expected_points: brief pause between groups if helpful
answer: 1. spell the vessel's call sign. Outcome: clear communication of the vessel's identity. Warning: ensure accurate spelling to avoid confusion.

question: Spell "MAYDAY" and "PAN PAN" when requested.
gold_answer: MAYDAY: MIKE-ALFA-YANKEE-DELTA-ALFA-YANKEE. PAN PAN: PAPA-ALFA-NOVEMBER, PAPA-ALFA-NOVEMBER. Note that in practice these prefixes are transmitted as words (MAYDAY x3, PAN PAN x3) not letter by letter. Being able to spell them accurately confirms familiarity with the phonetic alphabet.
expected_points: MAYDAY = MIKE ALFA YANKEE DELTA ALFA YANKEE
words are the prefixes themselves in practice
answer: The excerpt covers the procedures for making distress calls using VHF marine radio. Outcome: successful communication of distress information. Warning: do not forget to spell out 'MAYDAY' or 'PAN PAN' if not heard.

question: Demonstrate giving a latitude and longitude including degrees and minutes using words and numbers.
gold_answer: Example: "LATITUDE FIVE ZERO DEGREES ONE TWO DECIMAL FIVE MINUTES NORTH, LONGITUDE ZERO ZERO ONE DEGREES FOUR FIVE DECIMAL THREE MINUTES WEST, OVER." Digit by digit; use DECIMAL not POINT; state DEGREES, MINUTES and hemisphere (NORTH/SOUTH, EAST/WEST) in plain language.
expected_points: DEGREES and MINUTES stated in plain language
answer: 1. give latitude and longitude in degrees and minutes. Outcome: clear communication of position. Warning: ensure accuracy in position reporting.

question: Spell the name of a local hazard (e.g., "ROCKY SHOAL") so another vessel can note it correctly.
gold_answer: Example: "HAZARD NAME ROCKY SHOAL, I SPELL ROMEO-OSCAR-CHARLIE-KILO-YANKEE, ROCKY, SIERRA-HOTEL-OSCAR-ALFA-LIMA, SHOAL, OVER." Two-word hazard names are spelled as two separate I SPELL sequences with a brief pause between. This lets the receiving station write each word correctly.
expected_points: clear pronunciation of the whole name
answer: 1. spell the name of the local hazard. Outcome: other vessels can correctly identify and avoid the hazard. Warning: ensure all names of hazards are spelt clearly to avoid confusion.

question: Practice changing from normal speech to phonetic spelling and back smoothly in one transmission.
gold_answer: Example: "THIS IS (Vessel), WE ARE HEADING FOR CALSHOT, I SPELL CHARLIE-ALFA-LIMA-SIERRA-HOTEL-OSCAR-TANGO, CALSHOT, ETA ONE FIVE THREE ZERO UTC, OVER." The transition is signalled by the plain word first, I SPELL, then phonetic, then plain word again — after which normal speech continues seamlessly.
answer: 1. practice changing between normal speech and phonetic spelling. Outcome: improved clarity in communication during emergencies. Warning: do not use phonetic spelling unless requested by the other station.

question: Spell the name of a crew member to be evacuated to ensure hospital receives the correct details.
gold_answer: Example crew member ANDERSON, first name PAUL: "CASUALTY SURNAME ANDERSON, I SPELL ALFA-NOVEMBER-DELTA-ECHO-ROMEO-SIERRA-OSCAR-NOVEMBER, ANDERSON. FIRST NAME PAUL, I SPELL PAPA-ALFA-UNIFORM-LIMA, PAUL. AGE FIVE FOUR YEARS, MALE, OVER." Spelling both names is essential in SAR / MEDEVAC so hospital and family records are correct.
expected_points: critical for hospital and family records
answer: 1. spell the name clearly. Outcome: the hospital receives accurate information about the injured person. Warning: incorrect spelling may lead to confusion in medical assistance.

question: Spell a medical condition name provided by the examiner for a MEDICO scenario.
gold_answer: Example condition APPENDICITIS: "SUSPECTED CONDITION APPENDICITIS, I SPELL ALFA-PAPA-PAPA-ECHO-NOVEMBER-DELTA-INDIA-CHARLIE-INDIA-TANGO-INDIA-SIERRA, APPENDICITIS, OVER." Medical condition names are often unfamiliar to non-native speakers; spelling ensures a correct link to the duty doctor's diagnosis and advice.
answer: The excerpt provides communication phrases for a MEDICO scenario regarding medical advice and patient information. Outcome: effective communication of medical advice and patient status. Warning: do not omit important details when reporting medical conditions.

question: Spell the name of your marina or yacht club clearly for a radio log or report.
gold_answer: Example: "MARINA CROUCH HARBOUR, I SPELL CHARLIE-ROMEO-OSCAR-UNIFORM-CHARLIE-HOTEL, CROUCH, HOTEL-ALFA-ROMEO-BRAVO-OSCAR-UNIFORM-ROMEO, HARBOUR, OVER." Two-word names get two separate I SPELL sequences. This makes the log entry unambiguous.
answer: Pronunciation is important in VHF communication. Outcome: clear communication regarding the name and location of the marina. Warning: ensure pronunciation is clear to avoid confusion.

question: Spell a buoy identification code (e.g., "BF3") using phonetic and number words.
gold_answer: Example: "BUOY BF3, I SPELL BRAVO-FOXTROT, THREE, BF3, OVER." Letters spelled phonetically, digits with radiotelephony pronunciation. The plain code before and after the spelling confirms the whole.
answer: 1. spell the buoy identification code. Outcome: clear communication of the buoy's name and position. Warning: ensure accurate spelling to avoid confusion.

question: Demonstrate confirming a spelled-out course (e.g., "course 2 - 7 - 0") with readback.
gold_answer: Example: (Coastguard): "(Vessel), THIS IS (Coastguard), STEER COURSE TWO-SEVEN-ZERO, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), READBACK: STEER COURSE TWO-SEVEN-ZERO, OVER." (Coastguard): "ROGER, OUT." Each digit spoken separately; readback confirms accurate reception of a course that could otherwise be misheard as 220, 250 or 290.
expected_points: digit by digit for the course
answer: 1. confirm the course. Outcome: clear communication of the course being steered. Warning: ensure the course is confirmed to avoid navigation errors.

question: Spell the word "ANCHORAGE" on request.
gold_answer: "ANCHORAGE, I SPELL ALFA-NOVEMBER-CHARLIE-HOTEL-OSCAR-ROMEO-ALFA-GOLF-ECHO, ANCHORAGE, OVER." Plain word first, I SPELL, phonetic letters, plain word again. Standard technique for any unfamiliar or long English word.
expected_points: ALFA NOVEMBER CHARLIE HOTEL OSCAR ROMEO ALFA GOLF ECHO
answer: The excerpt covers communication phrases related to anchoring and berthing operations. Outcome: effective communication during anchoring and berthing operations. Warning: ensure all crew members are aware of the anchorage area before letting go the anchor.

question: Spell the name of a nearby vessel with a similar-sounding name to your own.
gold_answer: Example own vessel SEAWIND, nearby vessel SEAWEED: "NEARBY VESSEL SEAWEED, I SPELL SIERRA-ECHO-ALFA-WHISKEY-ECHO-ECHO-DELTA, SEAWEED, OVER." The phonetic spelling makes the distinction between similar-sounding names explicit so MRCC or the coastguard cannot confuse the two.
expected_points: essential when own and other vessel names are similar
answer: 1. spell the name of the vessel. Outcome: clear communication of the vessel's name. Warning: ensure the name is spelled correctly to avoid confusion.

question: Demonstrate teaching another crew member the phonetic alphabet in a short coaching scenario.
gold_answer: Sit at the radio and hand the crew member the laminated phonetic-alphabet card. Ask them to spell three easy items (the vessel's name, the port of destination, their own surname) and give positive feedback. Then run a mock exchange where you request a spelled position: "SAY AGAIN AND SPELL YOUR POSITION." Keep the coaching under 10 minutes and end with a hands-on drill.
expected_points: practise on vessel name, destination and own surname
mock exchange with SAY AGAIN AND SPELL
answer: 1. teach the phonetic alphabet. Outcome: improved communication clarity during distress situations. Warning: ensure all crew members understand the phonetic alphabet.

question: Perform a short simulated exchange where correct phonetic spelling prevents a navigational error.
gold_answer: Scenario: pilotage instruction from harbour to a small vessel. (Harbour): "(Vessel), STEER FOR NORTH CARDINAL WHISKEY PAPA, I SPELL WHISKEY-PAPA, THEN TURN STARBOARD INTO WEST HARBOUR, OVER." (Vessel): "THIS IS (Vessel), READBACK: STEER FOR NORTH CARDINAL WHISKEY PAPA, THEN TURN STARBOARD INTO WEST HARBOUR, OVER." (Harbour): "ROGER, OUT." Without the phonetic spelling of WP, the vessel could confuse it with WB, WD or KP and steer for a wrong buoy — potentially into shoal water.
expected_points: harbour uses I SPELL for buoy label
phonetic prevents confusion of similar letters
prevents grounding on wrong-buoy navigation error
answer: 1. spell out numbers and names clearly. Outcome: improved clarity in communication regarding numbers and names. Warning: incorrect pronunciation of numbers may lead to navigational errors.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Conduct a complete simulated MAYDAY exchange with MRCC from initial alert to coordination of assistance.
gold_answer: Sequence: (1) DSC distress alert on Ch 70 with nature and position; (2) voice MAYDAY on Ch 16 with full standard message (identity, position, nature, assistance, POB, OVER); (3) MRCC acknowledges and asks for follow-up detail (POB, injuries, safety equipment); (4) MRCC tasks assisting vessels and/or SAR units; (5) periodic updates on situation; (6) shift to working channel if MRCC directs; (7) situation resolved and MRCC terminates with SEELONCE FEENEE. All exchanges logged with UTC time.
expected_points: tasks assisting vessels and SAR units
periodic updates and shift to working channel
answer: 1. conduct a MAYDAY exchange. Outcome: effective communication of distress information. Warning: ensure all safety equipment is operational before departure.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Perform a PAN PAN call regarding a crew member with a suspected broken arm, then coordinate medical advice.
gold_answer: On Ch 16: "PAN PAN MEDICO x3, ALL STATIONS x3, THIS IS (vessel x3), MMSI (…), POSITION (…), MEDICAL: MALE CREW MEMBER AGED THREE FIVE, FELL FROM STEP, SUSPECTED FRACTURE RIGHT FOREARM, CONSCIOUS, STABLE, WEARING LIFE JACKET, REQUEST MEDICAL ADVICE, POB FOUR, OVER." MRCC responds, may link to duty doctor who will give first-aid and evacuation advice. Follow instructions and log everything.
expected_points: PAN PAN MEDICO x3, ALL STATIONS x3
request medical advice; MRCC connects duty doctor
answer: 1. make a PAN PAN call. 2. request medical advice. Outcome: medical assistance is provided to the injured crew member. Warning: ensure the injured person is not moved unless in danger.

section_title: Ability to Exchange Communications Relevant to the Safety of Life at Sea
question: Demonstrate using VHF to coordinate with a nearby vessel assisting you in a man-overboard recovery.
